## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The guide takes the explicit position that how an agency responds to an unintended outcome — accident, near-miss, or surprising non-accident — determines whether the organisation actually learns from it [AR] (Part 1, "Systems Thinking"). The traditional response — find who broke the rule, blame them, return the system to safety — is described as "not only ineffective for improving safety related to a specific accident, but also damaging to the overall learning culture" [V] (Part 1, "Systems Thinking"). The guide's organising claim is that learning requires a coherent stance built from three intertwined foundational principles: *Just Culture* (the work environment of trust, fairness and dignity in which honest accounts can be given), *Systems Thinking* (examination of the policies, procedures, processes and culture that shaped the conditions around an event, rather than the individual at the sharp end), and *Learning* (the treatment of unintended outcomes as a "valued learning opportunity and as a means to reducing uncertainty of future outcomes") [AR] (Part 1, "Systems Thinking"; Part 1, "Just Culture"; Part 1, "Learning").

A second load-bearing claim is that human performance variability is the rule, not the exception, and that adaptation and innovation are what produces successful outcomes most of the time. "It is impossible to predict all the potential situations that will arise in complex systems, and people are relied upon to make sense of these emerging conditions, learn in the moment, and innovate and adapt solutions to fit the situation" [V] (Part 1, "Part 1 – Foundational Principles"). "Employees make mistakes, but most of the time (almost continuously) they are actually *creating safety*" [V] (Part 1, "Part 1 – Foundational Principles"). The guide treats "human performance variability" as "not only normal, it's the rule" [V] (Part 1, "Learning").

A third load-bearing claim is that causal statements must be avoided in the FLA and that recommendations, in many circumstances, actually interfere with learning in complex systems — formal recommendations belong in the *Learning Review* (a distinct, more expensive process), where they can be vetted if a Delegating Official is willing to own them, while suggestions on technical fixes may occasionally be appropriate in an FLA [AR] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"; Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"; Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors"). "FLAs must avoid causal statements" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "Cause isn't something investigators 'find' or 'discover'; cause is always something we create by recreating the event showing how certain anomalies led to the accident" [V] (Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors"). The replacement concept is *networked causality* — "the combined total of those conditions that collectively influenced the event or outcome" [V] (Glossary, "Networked causality").

A fourth load-bearing claim is that "the story" — a factual, sensory, perspective-faithful narrative reconstruction of how the event made sense to the participants at the time — is the central learning artefact of the FLA. "Storytelling is widely recognized by educators as the most effective tool for experiential teaching and leading cultural change within an organization" [V] (Part 8, "Why FLA Storytelling?"). "Cognitive scientists have shown that humans make sense of, and remember, 'facts' by attaching them to narratives (i.e., stories) that give them context and a sensory or emotional association" [V] (Part 8, "Why FLA Storytelling?"). "In this way, storytelling moves Lessons Learned into the vicarious experience of Lessons Lived" [V] (Part 8, "Why FLA Storytelling?").

The guide frames all four claims with two epigraphs before its Preface: errors are unavoidable and what matters is "what we do after making the error" [V] [BT] (Tavris and Aronson), and a safety system needs a reporting culture, for which "What is needed is a just culture" [V] [BT] (Reason) (Front matter, epigraphs).

## Front matter: epigraphs (PDF p. 2)

The guide opens with two epigraphs before its Preface. The first is from Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson's *Mistakes Were Made (but not by me)*: errors appear in every baseball box score, and "Errors are not desirable, of course, but everyone understands that they are unavoidable" [V] [BT]; "the test of a nation's character, and of an individual's integrity, does not depend on being error free. It depends on what we do after making the error" [V] [BT] (Front matter, epigraph, citing Tavris and Aronson 2007, p. 235). The second is from J. T. Reason's *Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents*: "Any safety system depends crucially on the willing participation of the workforce, the people in direct contact with the hazards. To achieve this, it is necessary to engineer a reporting culture—an organizational climate in which people are prepared to report their errors" [V] [BT]; the passage closes, "What is needed is a just culture" [V] [BT] (Front matter, epigraph, citing Reason 1997, p. 195). A photograph from the 2011 Salt Fire Entrapment and Shelter Deployment FLA carries a participant's words, "Get in This Truck!" [V] (Front matter, photo caption).

## Part I: The three foundational principles (Part 1)

### Systems Thinking — accidents as system-shaped, not person-caused

Systems thinking is presented as the alternative to the blame frame. "When an accident happens, system thinking enables us to examine how the organization's policies, procedures, processes and culture may have influenced the circumstances around the event" [V] (Part 1, "Systems Thinking"). The diagnostic question is framed in *work-as-imagined vs work-as-done* terms: "How were we actually completing the work vs how managers were expecting the work to be completed?" [V] (Part 1, "Systems Thinking"). "Systems thinking enables change in complex contexts by looking at the world in terms of wholes and relationships" [V] (Part 1, "Systems Thinking"). The Glossary entry confirms the framing with a definition it credits to Wikipedia: "a way of making sense of the complexity of the world by looking at it in terms of wholes and relationships rather than by splitting it down into its parts" [V] [BT] (Glossary, "Systems Thinking", attributed in the source to Wikipedia).

### Just Culture — forward-looking accountability over criminal-style culpability

Just Culture is defined as the intersection of trust, fairness, and dignity, with an open and safe reporting system in which "everyone can speak" [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture"). The guide draws an explicit contrast with criminal justice: "In the criminal justice arena accountability means punishments and correction. In our Just Culture, accountability means creating the space for each person involved to provide an honest account of what happened from his or her perspective" [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture"). The Glossary makes the etymology explicit: "Accountability: An account is something you tell and learn from" [V] (Glossary, "Accountability"). The guide also names the antonym slang: "Accountabilism: a slang term which refers to circumstances when an investigation or review effort claims the intent is to learn from participants sharing their 'accounts' but then punishes via judgmental language, requiring training or other organizational actions which punish" [V] (Glossary, "Accountabilism").

The just-culture framing is forward-looking: "This definition of just culture is focused on forward-looking accountability. It is concerned with sharing accounts of people involved in unintended outcomes to highlight the weaknesses and strengths in the system; to help us learn ways to improve ourselves. It is concerned with preventing the next accident, not focused on correcting history" [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture").

Restorative justice is named as a fourth component: "After a serious accident, employees are often emotionally harmed, and relationships can be strained or broken. With its focus on transparency and rejection of blame, the FLA process seeks to restore victims to wholeness" [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture"). "Restorative justice culture aims to repair trust and relationships damaged after an incident. It allows all parties to discuss how they have been affected and collaboratively decide how they want to proceed" [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture"). The guide points to Appendix F, "Restorative Justice Checklist", for more; the checklist is held in the PDF as page images, so it is described from an OCR of those pages in Part XIV below (Appendix F). Appendix A elaborates: "A mature just culture is characterized by openness and trust" [V] (Appendix A, "A Deeper Dive Into Just Culture"); "In a Just Culture, there is consensus among all employees that information (learning) is the lifeblood of safety" [V] (Appendix A, "A Deeper Dive Into Just Culture"). Two pull quotes sit beside the Just Culture section: "Trust is built in drops and lost in buckets" [V] [BT] (Part 1, "Just Culture", pull quote attributed to Kevin A. Plank), and, from Preston Cline, academic reviewer for the Eicks Learning Review, "In large organization and amidst bureaucratic complexity, there can be institutioned deception to believe that risks are being mitigated, when in fact they are just being traded for other types of unseen risks" [V] [BT] (Part 1, "Just Culture", pull quote; "institutioned" as printed). The Sidney Dekker / Hugh Breakey 2016 *Safety Science* paper on substantive, procedural, and restorative justice is cited as the academic source [BT] (Glossary, "Restorative justice", footnote 14).

A boxed passage in the Just Culture section names the attitude the FLA rejects. It quotes "You've got nothing to fear if you've done nothing wrong" [V] and answers: "Punishing or blaming employees involved in an accident is the surest way to kill a learning culture. The attitude expressed in the quote above is a threat and has no place in an FLA" [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture", box). Beneath it, a passage from Sidney Dekker's *Just Culture: Who Gets to Draw the Line?* (2008) separates accountability from blame: "Holding people accountable and blaming people are two quite different things. Blaming people may in fact make them less accountable: they will tell fewer accounts, they may feel less compelled to have their voice heard, to participate in improvement efforts. Blame-free or no-fault systems are not accountability-free systems" [V] [BT]; "If we see an act as a crime, then accountability means blaming and punishing somebody for it. Accountability in that case is backward-looking, retributive. If, instead, we see the act as an indication of an organizational, operational, technical, educational or political issue, then accountability can become forward-looking (Sharpe 2003)" [V] [BT] (Part 1, "Just Culture", box, quoting Dekker 2008).

### Learning — variability is the rule, not the exception

The Learning principle treats adaptation and innovation as continuous and normal rather than exceptional. "Errors, mistakes, and lapses are inherent in the human condition. So is taking shortcuts to save money, time, and effort as well as under and overestimating risk" [V] (Part 1, "Learning"). "Indeed, human performance variability is not only normal, it's the rule!" [V] (Part 1, "Learning"). The learning frame inverts the standard treatment of accidents: "If leaders recognize that this variability will always be a part of the overall organization, they can treat accidents and other unintended outcomes as precious opportunities to look deeply into the operation to better understand how employees perceive and manage risk" [V] (Part 1, "Learning").

Organisational learning is treated at multiple scales: grass-roots story-sharing (Mann Gulch, via Maclean's *Young Men and Fire*, is named as an example of narrative-mediated learning) [AE] (Part 1, "What is organizational learning?"); leadership-level adaptation of equipment, policy, and training (the Ten Standard Firefighting Orders, the fire shelter, and the Incident Command System are named as products of this level) [AE] (Part 1, "What is organizational learning?"); and complex FLAs / Learning Reviews with explicit Lessons Learned Analyses (Part 1, "What is organizational learning?"). As agencies build libraries of these reports, "leaders, safety professionals and policy analysts can review multiple documents and target policy change" [V] (Part 1, "What is organizational learning?"). Two pull quotes frame the section. Former Forest Service Chief Tom Tidwell: "I consider learning from events to be a Forest Service core value, both equally fundamental to prevention and critical to your safety" [V] [BT]. Ivan Pupulidy, retired Director of the Office of Innovation and Organizational Learning: "The focus of investigation shifts from judging actions or decisions as right or wrong and people as good or bad, to developing an understanding how worker actions can be tied to a network of influences, or performance shaping factors" [V] [BT]; the desired outcome is that "organizations purposefully increase their capacity to learn and workers recognize how important it is to learn their way through work" [V] [BT] (Part 1, "What is organizational learning?", pull quotes).

### Lineage — how the process got here

The historical section traces the lineage from criminal prosecution of firefighters after the Thirtymile and Cramer fatalities through the 2005 I-90 Tarkio Fire Entrapment learning-focused investigation, the 2006 "Peer Review" briefing paper, and the formal adoption of the FLA and Learning Review processes by the Forest Service in July 2013 [AP] (Part 1, "How we got here"). "In 2005, two members from the USFS Fire Operations Risk Management Council pushed the limits of policy by conducting a learning-focused serious accident investigation on the I-90 Tarkio Fire Entrapment" [V] (Part 1, "How we got here"). The section opens on the conditions that prompted the change: "By the end of 2004, the U.S. Forest Service fire community was stunned and disoriented by a string of administrative decisions and legal actions against firefighters involved in accidents" [V] (Part 1, "How we got here"). A pull quote from Tom Tidwell, from his introduction to the Coordinated Response Protocol safety-engagement website, states the commitment the process rests on: "The [accident] review information will not be used as a basis for disciplinary action, or to place blame on employees. I cannot stress this enough. An accident review is about learning, it is about understanding what happened so if possible, we can make changes to produce a different outcome in the future" [V] [BT] (Part 1, "How we got here", pull quote). A sidebar notes that "The products produced over the years reflect the evolving process as we continue to implement, evaluate and adapt the concepts explored in this guide" [V], and the Lessons Learned Center hosts a 25-minute introductory video on the FLA (Part 1, "How we got here"). The Thirtymile, Cramer, and Esperanza cluster is presented as a real-world illustration of what happens without a Just Culture: "Our employees were criminally prosecuted in the aftermath of the Thirtymile and Cramer fires because at the time, extremely complex problems were perceived as simple problems with simplistic solutions. Then our employees refused to talk to the accident investigation team looking into the Esperanza Fire fatalities because they did not feel like they were going to be treated fairly" [V] (Appendix A, "A Deeper Dive Into Just Culture").

## Part II: The four tools and how to choose between them (Part 2)

The guide identifies four distinct tools for responding to outcomes, scaling from immediate-local to organisational-system level.

**AAR (After-Action Review).** "A powerful tool to capture immediate, local learning. AARs are predominantly closed, personal, and confidential, enabling participants to speak freely about mistakes. The learning that occurs from an AAR typically is at the individual level, local in nature, not shared beyond the work unit (crew or team) and does not affect the organization as a whole" [V] (Part 2, "The tools"). The AAR's product stays inside the work unit; the involved group "moves on, goes back to work, while learning from mistakes and building on successes" [V] (Part 2, "The tools").

**RLS (Rapid Lessons Sharing).** Expands on the AAR by producing "a simple learning product — focused on a near-miss or accident, or a new tool, technique, process or protocol — that can be shared with anyone who might benefit" [V] (Part 2, "The tools"). The product usually takes the form of a one- or two-page narrative document with concrete, actionable lessons [AP] (Part 2, "The tools"). The Wildland Fire Lessons Learned Center hosts a submission tool through which people in the field can submit lessons, "anonymously if they wish" [V] (Part 2, "The tools").

**FLA (Facilitated Learning Analysis).** Has a signed delegation of authority "assuring participants that there shall be no punitive actions" [V] (Part 2, "The tools"). "An FLA is a scalable process used to make sense of an unintended outcome and develop lessons learned for the broader organization without recommendations" [V] (Part 2, "The tools"). Scales from a "basic FLA" (a couple of people, completed within a week) to a "complex FLA" (5 to 15 people including SMEs, working weeks or months) (Part 2, "The tools"). Output is a learning product — historically a written report, now expanding to multimedia.

**Learning Review.** "The key difference between the other tools and a LR is that the delegating authority for a LR has requested recommendations as an output of the review process" [V] (Part 2, "The tools"). The LR takes the FLA's product and adds community-of-practice focus groups (and, as an option, academic or professional subject-matter experts) and a Learning Review Board to vet and approve recommendations and produce a Safety Action Plan (Part 2, "The tools"; Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"; Part 11, "Learning Review Board").

The guide explicitly distinguishes the FLA/LR family from the Serious Accident Investigation (SAI) process used by DOI agencies: "the SAI process relies on a root cause analysis, where the FLA and Learning Review processes focuses on conditions and context surrounding the event and relies on the concept of networked causality" [V] (Part 2, "The tools").

A sidebar states the "Leader's Intent for an FLA": "An FLA is successful if it accurately captures the information about an event with enough detail to provide a picture of the incident so that the reader (or listener) can determine (on their own) why the actions made sense and the participants feel it represents their perspectives. The process does not require analysis or judgment; rather, it presents information like a documentary. An FLA is somewhat like a staff ride. Observations and recollections do not have to agree; in fact, the process should capture the fog of war" [V] (Part 2, "Leader's Intent for an FLA").

A boxed section, "What is all this talk about 'conditions'?", explains the term the whole process turns on. "Understanding conditions of influence is extremely important to the FLA process. These conditions often form the basis of the analysis part of the FLA process" [V]. Employees often hear "conditions" as weather or topography, but "they are only a small subset of the conditions we are looking for. An FLA seeks to understand the organizational, social, cultural, and other conditions that were present when the event happened" [V]. Understanding them "can help us get a better grasp of the pressures, goal conflicts, and other factors that affected the pertinent decisions and actions that took place during the event" [V], and "will aid in making systemic improvements to improve the way we engage in normal work every day" [V] (Part 2, "What is all this talk about 'conditions'?"). The box names Erik Hollnagel's efficiency/thoroughness trade-off as one way to recognise conditions of influence: "He argues that trade-offs between thoroughness and efficiency are made in almost every situation in almost all environments, almost continuously" [V] [BT], and recommends *The ETTO Principle* to those interested in FLAs (Part 2, "What is all this talk about 'conditions'?").

## Part III: Delegating Official decisions before the team forms (Part 3)

The Delegating Official's job, before a team is formed, is to choose a process and write its delegation of authority. The selection criterion the guide warns against is severity-of-outcome alone — "the natural tendency is to base the size and complexity of the review team upon the severity of the outcome. Often, the more 'serious the accident,' the more resources are put toward the review team. This tendency may pretermit stellar learning opportunities" [V] (Part 3, "Starting the process"). The illustrative case is a tree-cutting accident in which a firefighter was knocked unconscious by a glancing blow and released the same day. "Based solely on the outcome, this wasn't considered a 'significant' accident" [V] (Part 3, "Starting the process"); the guide argues that had the tree fallen one or two inches to the left, the firefighter would have been killed or seriously and probably permanently injured, and that the choice to learn or not learn should not depend on a chance occurrence of two inches [AE] (Part 3, "Starting the process"; Part 3, "Questions to consider when deciding to mobilize a team").

A sidebar, "The GAP: Advice to Delegating Officials", turns the same point into a sizing rule. "The most intriguing part of this 'Gap' is the difference between how much risk employees are taking in getting their work done—compared to how much risk administrators would say is acceptable" [V]. A large gap, shown by "shock and awe when it is revealed (usually in the wake of an accident)" [V], is illustrated with a quote from David Woods: "The future seems implausible before an accident. . . But after the accident, the past seems incredible" [V] [BT] (Part 3, "The GAP: Advice to Delegating Officials"). The advice: "The greater the gap between the level of risk acceptance by employees and risk acceptability by managers, the more resources, time, and effort should be put into the accident review" [V] (Part 3, "The GAP: Advice to Delegating Officials"). The same pages point Delegating Officials to Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?", and note that "Often the reason for conducting the FLA turns out to be fairly simple and instead the response to the accident becomes the focus of the Lessons Learned" [V], as in the 2012 Wenatchee Complex Faller Fatality FLA [AE] (Part 3, sidebars).

The decision-support questions (Part 3, "Questions to consider when deciding to mobilize a team") are eleven: how "deep" will you look (the specific set of events, or deeper organisational opportunities)? is there enough trust here to support such an analysis? how might we exploit this event to make an impact on organisational safety? what kinds of specialised subject-matter experts might be needed? how long should this take, and how much time and money are we willing to spend? are there conflicting stories surrounding the event? regardless of the outcome, do people close to the accident believe it could have been much more severe? what could be the cost of not choosing an FLA in terms of opportunities lost? how close are you to the incident, and how much do you own the decisions? are recommendations going to be an essential part of this report (necessitating a learning review)? what other jurisdictions or agencies are involved, and is an interagency agreement on accident investigations needed to determine team composition? [AP]

The guide makes a critical scope-extension explicit: "The AAR, RLS, FLA and LR processes were designed to be tools for accident investigation and learning from accident-like unintended outcomes. We should use the applicable process to review events that surprise us to make sense of the events and try to learn from them. However, these are also tools that have been used successfully to learn from events that were not accidents; including close call/near-miss events and events that weren't necessarily negative but had outcomes surprising to administrators" [V] (Part 3, "Learning beyond accidents"). The named examples include the Retardant Avoidance FLA, the Bear Meadows Stop Work FLA, the Burdette Fire Case Study, the Mud Lake Complex FLA, the Area Command COVID-19 FLA, and the "How Do We Honor the Fallen?" review [AE] (Part 3, "Learning beyond accidents"). A sidebar states that complex FLAs and Learning Reviews meet all accident-investigation requirements: "An FLA and Learning Review meet the serious accident investigation procedural and documentation requirements of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's (OSHA) Executive Order 12196, Public Law 107302, Title 5, USC 7902 as well as the accident investigation regulations (29 CFR 1960.29, 29 CFR 1904.2, 41 CFR 101-37 and 49 CFR 830 NTSB) and internal policies of the U.S. Forest Service" [V] (Part 3, "Complex FLAs and Learning Reviews Meet All 'Accident Investigation' Requirements").

The administrative-firewall commitment is formalised as: "It is critical to maintain a solid firewall between the FLA and any potential administrative actions that may be taken against the employee. Information is the lifeblood of safety. We must cherish it and protect it" [V] (Part 3, "Administrative assurance of no punitive actions"). Administrative actions to be excluded include "any type of disciplinary actions and other adverse actions such as forced retraining, removal from an incident or reduction in planned overtime" [V] (Part 3, "Administrative assurance of no punitive actions"). The Delegating Official cannot, however, offer immunity from external legal action.

The guide names *fundamental attribution error* as the cognitive trap of blaming employees: "Blaming employees can be a form of the Fundamental Attribution Error" [V] (Part 3, "Administrative assurance of no punitive actions"). It cites Hollnagel's ETTO principle for the underlying tension: "Our employees always face conflicting goals and tensions between production and efficiency" [V] (Part 3, "Administrative assurance of no punitive actions"), footnoted to *The ETTO Principle Efficiency-Thoroughness Trade-Off* [BT] (Part 3, footnote 2). A Dekker pull quote sits beside the section: "In a just culture, management can balance the tension between needing to know what is going on, and needing to correct what is going on" [V] [BT] (Part 3, "Administrative assurance of no punitive actions", pull quote). The facing page carries a quote from the Fire Operations Risk Management Council: "Hindsight bias is the chief saboteur of any accident investigation. Interviewers should remember their highest objective, to be able to describe how interviewees (the people they are interviewing) developed their understanding of the situation—and then made sense of their choices at the time, and in context" [V], and a captioned photograph naming the 2008 Elkhorn 2 Escaped Prescribed Fire FLA as "one of the first attempts to use the FLA process to fulfill the requirement for Escaped Prescribed Fire Reviews" [V] [AE] (Part 3, pull quote and photo caption; the caption's last sentence is cut off by its frame in the PDF).

### The FLA process at a glance (Part 4)

Part 4 is a single graphic, "a broad overview of the FLA process that can take place in 1-2 days or over several months" [V] (Part 4, "The FLA process"). It starts from "Something happens that we seek a greater understanding about…" [V] and runs through numbered steps, each pointing to the Part of the guide that covers it [AP] (Part 4, graphic; step order read from a render of PDF p. 22, because the converted text gives the labels in drawing order):

1. **AAR RLS FLA LR** — "Reach out to RMO or Safety Manager to discuss the most appropriate tool" [V] (Part 2).
2. **Initiate the Process** — "Form the Team, provide a delegation, set-up introductions and in-briefing" [V] (Parts 3 and 5).
3. **Interact with the Participants** — "The site visit, interviews and group dialogue session are all options for this part of the process" [V] (Part 6).
4. **Bringing it all together** — "Event/accident reconstructions writing a story and creating a learning product are all options" [V] (Parts 7, 8 and 9).
5. **Readbacks and Editing** — "Checking in with participants, seeking their edits and validating their story is a critical part of the process" [V] (Parts 7, 8 and 9).
6. **Brief Delegating Official** — "The Team works with FLA coach on how to proceed" [V] (Appendix D); "If recommendations are desired, see Step 7" [V].
7. **Learning Review Process** — "Building upon the story construction from the FLA process, focus groups are formed for dialogue and formation of recommendations" [V] (Parts 10 and 11).

## Part IV: Forming the FLA team (Part 5)

After the Delegating Official's pre-decisions, Part 5 specifies team composition. Pre-team priorities are *take care of employees* (CISM, EAP, Family/Hospital Liaisons), *assign liaisons* (a trusted employee point of contact who can explain the process), and *manage concurrent investigations* (claims, prescribed fire reviews, law enforcement) (Part 5, "Priority Delegating Official Actions").

On taking care of employees: after a critical incident "it is the responsibility of the Delegating Official to ensure that the appropriate support needs are provided for the employee, their families, co-workers and others impacted" [V] (Part 5, "Take Care of Employees"). Response often includes a CISM Team "comprised of Peer Supporters and Clinicians specially trained in stress management" [V], and the Employee Assistance Program is another tool [AP]; "The FLA Team lead may need to coordinate with CISM (or related efforts) regarding interviewing participants" [V] (Part 5, "Take Care of Employees"). Family Liaisons and Hospital Liaisons, used after a fatality or serious hospitalisation, "aid in bridging the gap between the Agency and the employee and/or employee's family and to help ease their burden" [V] (Part 5, "Take Care of Employees").

On liaisons: "Provide employees with a trusted liaison who can explain the FLA process and who will be available to support employees until the FLA is completed" [V] (Part 5, "Assign Liaison(s)"). "Employees will have questions and concerns about what is happening" [V]; "When personnel are waiting post-accident they can have high levels of anxiety about what is going to happen next; it will be very important to provide them with real-time information and answer their questions" [V] (Part 5, "Assign Liaison(s)"). On wildland fire incidents the liaison also tries to keep critical employees or contractors from being demobilised (or gathers their contact details) before the team is ready, and can help the team with logistics and travel [AP] (Part 5, "Assign Liaison(s)").

On concurrent investigations: a separate claims investigation should occur where there is significant private property damage or personal injury, and prescribed fire reviews or law enforcement investigations need coordination "to minimize impacts on employees and streamline information gathering" [V]; "Each situation is unique so there is no prescriptive method to follow" [V] (Part 5, "Concurrent Investigations").

Note-taking guidance is grounded in memory research: "Research tells us that memories change; perspectives shift as time progresses. Research also shows us that memories are unreliable and its important to try to capture thoughts as quick as possible after an event" [V] (Part 5, "Should the affected people take Notes?"). Personal notes remain the employee's property; they will not be collected or read by anyone else.

The Delegating Official forms the FLA team with their safety and/or risk advisors. "The general rule is that the more surprised the supervisors and agency leaders are in the outcome and/or the risks employees were accepting, the richer the potential harvest of learning can be by opting for an FLA team" [V] (Part 5, "Forming the FLA team").

A boxed section asks the Delegating Official, "Are you the elephant in the room?": "As the person responsible for requesting an FLA, is it possible that you—your decisions, guidance and leadership—are one of the key influences that need to be examined in the course of the FLA?" [V] (Part 5, "Are you the elephant in the room?"). It reports that "A December 2014 analysis of FLA products highlighted a significant finding: FLAs tend to not include an examination of the decisions made by Delegating Officials and other key supervisors. This analysis also indicates that most FLAs tend to focus almost solely on actions and actors at the scene" [V] [AR]. Examining those closest to the incident ("the 'tip of the spear'") is critical, "it is also critical that we examine the strategic and organizational influences and conditions that contributed to their outcomes" [V]. The Delegating Official "may need to be deliberate about ensuring that the FLA team includes you, as well as other key supervisors and strategic-level decision-makers in the FLA process" [V], and one way to begin is to ask the team, through the Delegation of Authority letter, "to examine this deceivingly complex question: 'Why were they there?'" [V] (Part 5, "Are you the elephant in the room?"). Part 6 points back to this box when it tells teams to interview project leaders, supervisors and Delegating Officials (Part 6, "Participants").

Minimum team-member attributes (Part 5, "Forming the FLA team"):

- A basic understanding of Just Culture.
- A basic understanding of the FLA process (team leaders and facilitators should be formally trained or have experience under a trainer).
- A solid reputation for dealing with confidential matters.
- It is better not to have members from the local unit (or to be aware of the bias they bring if local members are used).
- Selection of Team Leader and Facilitator should consider the individual's ability to extricate themselves from the incident to avoid inputting personal bias into the process.

Roles listed (Part 5, "Potential FLA team members and roles"): FLA Process Coach, Learning Review Process Coach, Team Leader (the delegated official, accountable for quality and content), Lead Facilitator (the FLA process expert, analogous to "chief investigator" on a Serious Accident Investigation Team), Storyteller/Writer-Editor (a creative-nonfiction writer where one is available), Subject-Matter Experts/Peers (current peer to the affected role), Technical Specialists, NTDP equipment SMEs (mandatory consultation if PPE / burnover / shelter deployment is involved), the National Chainsaw Program Manager (mandatory for tree-falling/chainsaw accidents), the Missoula Fire Lab (for escape-route / safety-zone events), Human Performance experts via the Office of Innovation and Organizational Learning (IOL), FARO LIDAR operators (typically law-enforcement-community), Videographers and graphic designers, Union Representative (NFFE has been a strong supporter of Just Culture and the FLA process), Interagency Participation members, and Documentation Specialist (for complex FLAs with likely litigation). Like the Incident Command System, FLA teams are "a changeable, scalable response organization" [V]; one or two people can cover every role on a small FLA, and roles are split out as complexity grows [AP] (Part 5, "Potential FLA team members and roles"). Several role descriptions carry load: "The delegation of authority is issued to the team leader, who is ultimately the responsible official accountable for the quality and content of the FLA" [V] (Part 5, "Team Leader"); "A primary duty of the Lead Facilitator is to flesh out the conditions or influences that led to decisions and actions" [V] (Part 5, "Lead Facilitator"); "The most effective way to share the learning throughout the organization is with a powerful story" [V] (Part 5, "Storyteller/Writer-Editor"); a peer must hold "current, intimate knowledge of the duties and skills necessary to serve in a similar position/job title" [V], so an engine rollover calls for someone currently on an engine crew [AE] (Part 5, "Subject-Matter Experts/Peers"). Upon request a union representative sits with employees during all interviews [AP] (Part 5, "Union Representative"). A sidebar lists the NTDP team's subject areas: PPE and equipment, all aviation-related work (smokejumper, helicopter rappel, short haul, UAS), helicopter missions (sling, longline, hooks), fireline PPE including the fire shelter, ignition equipment, fuel geysering, water-handling equipment, crew carriers and engines, and physiological impacts (HRI, rhabdo) [AP] (Part 5, "NTDP SMEs" sidebar). "A Brief Sidebar about Data" points teams to a form, developed with Joint Fire Science Program Project 18-S-01-1 and the Wildland Fire Histomap project, that collects variables on incidents, accidents and burnover entrapments, from a GPS point to fuels, weather and topography [AP] (Part 5, "A Brief Sidebar about Data"). Where property damage or injury could bring claims or litigation years later, "the FLA document may be the government's only official accident investigation report" [V] (Part 5, "Documentation Specialist").

The Common Operating Picture between FLA team and host unit is established through four items (Part 5, "A Common Operating Picture" through "Cooperation with Other Investigations"):

- **Clear mutual objectives.** The team in-briefs with the delegating authority and then with the individuals involved, to set expectations for the coming days or weeks and what the outcome of the review will look like [AP]; "Always be wary of host unit expectations for a 'quick wrap-up.'" [V]. The delegating authority and the team review the delegation of authority together, along with each item in Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?" [AP] (Part 5, "Clear Mutual Objectives").
- **Understand the fundamentals.** Everyone should understand how an FLA differs from other investigations and be assured that no administrative punitive actions will result; "This assurance of no agency imposed administrative actions must be clearly stated in the delegation to the FLA Team Leader" [V] (Part 5, "Understand the Fundamentals"). If the team learns someone acted with a willful and reckless disregard for human safety, "the FLA Team Leader will likely terminate the FLA and advise the delegating authority that an administrative review is a more appropriate tool" [V], and "The FLA Team Leader must not disclose any details to the delegating authority other than a recommendation to pursue an administrative or law enforcement investigation" [V] (Part 5, "Understand the Fundamentals"). A boxed line sets the limit of the assurance: "All participants must understand that the assurance of no administrative action does not protect employees against actions taken by the Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General, or other authorities that are outside the control of the agency" [V] (Part 5, "Understand the Fundamentals").
- **Trust.** "All FLA team members must guard this trust and never betray the confidentiality of the employees involved or divulge any information not contained in the learning product to anyone outside the team" [V]; the only exception is a judicial order outside agency control [AP] (Part 5, "Trust").
- **Cooperation with other investigations.** "FLAs are independent from other investigations or reviews that may be occurring" [V]; communications with the people involved, internal team deliberations and draft learning products are held confidential to the extent possible [AP]. OSHA or OIG investigations are supported by the Delegating Official but kept separate from the FLA process and team members; evidentiary material (photographs, dispatch-log transcripts, law enforcement reports, PPE) must be shared when requested, with requests routed through the Delegating Official [AP]. "Interaction directly between the FLA team and OSHA, agency law enforcement, or any other investigative authority should be limited to the FLA team leader. Other members of the FLA team should be insulated from this potential influence" [V] (Part 5, "Cooperation with Other Investigations"). To introduce the different teams to those involved, "A way to do this that has been successful in the past is to conduct a 'Morning Briefing' where the leaders of each of the investigation teams present themselves to a group of interviewees and explains/describes their respective objectives" [V] (Part 5, "Cooperation with Other Investigations").

A sidebar beside the list, "Open, Frequent Communication", adds: "Regularly scheduled conversations should occur between the FLA Team Leader and the agency official who authorized the FLA" [V], for two purposes: "To keep the agency official updated on the FLA team's progress, and" "To ensure that the FLA is meeting the needs of the delegating official" [V]. "These conversations are not an opportunity for the Delegating Official to 'steer' the analysis in a particular direction. Rather, they are opportunities to ensure that the needs of the official are being met and that the FLA Team is answering all of the 'how' and 'why' questions that initially triggered the review" [V] (Part 5, "Open, Frequent Communication").

### Recommendations vs lessons learned — the central design choice

The "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned" section is one of the guide's most argument-dense (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "The old investigation paradigm has been that we prevent accidents by discovering their root cause, and then fixing the cause to prevent a repeat of the accident. This perspective is problematic in complex systems and highly subjective because they are always outcome dependent" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "There can always be room for improvement, but we must remember that an accident represents a single data point with a single outcome. FLAs must avoid causal statements" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned").

The argument against recommendations as the default output is that "Managers used to the 'causal' model may jump straight to the 'Recommendations' section of the learning product, develop an action plan, and believe they've solved the problem. Readers may look to recommendations for security, 'If I'm following these recommendations, then I must be safe.' In both cases, our cultural baggage around recommendations may make learning harder because there is no zero-risk option to complete work" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned").

"In many circumstances, recommendations actually interfere with learning. Often recommendations, when implemented, add complexity to the workplace, which has the paradoxical effect of increasing risk" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). The guide's preferred alternative is to "consider ways to make the FLA learning product an effective and compelling learning tool" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"), with Hollnagel's ETTO principle cited as the underlying frame (Part 5, footnote 4): "Often, the best outcome of an accident investigation or an FLA is learning how we make sense of risk and the tensions between efficiency and thoroughness" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "In lieu of written recommendations in the process, the Team Leader can discuss recommendations informally with the Delegating Officials" [V], a point to cover in the delegation of authority letter [AP] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "On occasion, providing suggestions on technical fixes may be appropriate" [V]; a chainsaw specialist's way to avoid chainsaw fuel geysers could go in the learning product or a stand-alone technical report [AE] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned").

The position is not absolute. "If the Delegating Official insists on having recommendations, the Learning Review process must be initiated so the recommendations can be vetted with the communities of practice and a Safety Action Plan can be developed that outlines who is responsible to carry them out and by what date" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "We argue against providing recommendations on the basis of a single data point" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "The team is strongly encouraged to share lessons the participants learned and intend to implement for themselves in the future, but not formal recommendations others should be compelled to follow" [V]; "recommendations people are compelled to use without taking into account specific contexts can be problematic" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). Systemic issues that emerge during an FLA are passed to the assigned Process Coach to aid organisational improvement [AP] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned").

Part 5 closes on human performance expertise: in some FLAs "the emphasis on speed over thoroughness comes at a high cost in terms of lost opportunity to involve specialists, particularly human performance experts" [V] (Part 5, "Human Performance Expertise").

A boxed section closes Part 5: "When Do We Transition from a Basic FLA to a Complex FLA or to a Learning Review?" At the outset, "the FLA team and the Delegating Official should agree (at least in principle) on the bounds of the FLA. That is, how long it will take, the complexity of the analysis, how the report will appear, etc." [V]. "Usually, this first assessment of the size and complexity of the FLA team is correct. Often, additional time is needed but it is rare for additional team members to be required" [V]. "Occasionally, a team will uncover a surprise, a rich vein of learning opportunities" [V], which may need technical experts, a human performance expert or a storyteller, each adding cost, complexity and time, and "The team and the Delegating Official may need to modify the delegation of authority to explore more fully a gap that has been revealed" [V]. "To shift from a basic or moderately complex FLA to a much more thorough and complex analysis is difficult but can be absolutely necessary. Team members that committed to a week may have to spend a month. A unit that budgeted a few thousand dollars for an FLA may have to come up with tens of thousands. There is no easy answer to these issues. Frequent, open communication will make them easier to deal with" [V] (Part 5, "When Do We Transition from a Basic FLA to a Complex FLA or to a Learning Review?"). A sidebar gives the Gregg Creek FLA team's video of the 2015 Gregg Creek Fire as an example of a learning resource beyond the written report [AE] (Part 5, sidebar).

## Part V: Engaging the process — site visits, interviews, group dialogue (Part 6)

The heart of the FLA process is described as "dialogue with the participants" [V] (Part 6, "Site visits, Interviews and Group Dialogue sessions"). Three engagement modalities — site visits, individual interviews, and the facilitated group dialogue — are treated as the means through which the foundational principles are put into practice.

### Setting the stage and giving participants control

"Throughout the FLA process, team members should be prepared to explain the history of FLA and its major underpinnings, such as the degree of confidentiality, Just Culture and The Gap" [V] (Part 6, "Setting the stage"). "Delegating Officials and FLA participants may not be familiar with the process; there is also a tendency after an incident for participants to worry that this time the 'investigators' are out to get them. A frank discussion of the delegation can be useful to frame the conversation and to give assurance about the Delegating Official's stance on punitive action" [V] (Part 6, "Setting the stage"). "Explaining the process can help put them at ease and make them more responsive through the process" [V] (Part 6, "Setting the stage"). The "Gap" is defined in the Glossary as "the difference between what administrators think is going on and what is really going on in the field" [V] (Glossary, "GAP").

"For both individual and group dialogue sessions, the team should attempt to provide as comfortable environment as possible. Perhaps the best way to accomplish this is to give as much control as possible to the participants" [V] (Part 6, "Site visits, Interviews and Group Dialogue sessions"). The practical examples — engine barn, saw shop, tac shed, picnic tables — are framed as ways to keep participants from "feeling like they are being interrogated" [V] (Part 6, "Site visits, Interviews and Group Dialogue sessions"). A pull quote from William Isaacs's *Dialogue and the Art of Thinking Together* sits beside it: "In skillful discussion, we inquire into the reasons behind someone's position and the thinking and the evidence to support it. As this kind of discussion progresses, it can lead to a dialectic, the productive antagonism of two points of view. A dialectic pits different ideas against one another and then makes space for new views to emerge out of both" [V] [BT] (Part 6, pull quote). A captioned photo notes that "One place to conduct interviews is at the accident site" [V], as in the 2006 Little Venus Entrapment [AE] (Part 6, "Site Visits", caption).

### Interviews

"The intent of an interview is to capture the person's story" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). For a basic FLA the facilitator may have enough background to go straight to the dialogue, but "Most often however, key people involved in the accident should be interviewed before the group dialogue session" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). For complex FLAs, extensive interviewing "should not be hurried to meet an arbitrary date" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). "Interviews should occur as soon after the accident as possible, especially for accident victims who demonstrate a strong emotional response to the event" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). "For key accident participants or witnesses, the team leader should consider using a team of two interviewers. One interviewer will take notes, while the other engages the participant" [V]; the caveat is that "because using two interviewers can sometimes be intimidating to the interviewee, this approach should be used with appropriate caution and understanding" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). Participants more tangential to the accident may be interviewed in groups of two to four [AP] (Part 6, "Interviews"). A sidebar gives "Tips for success": "Control the interview environment" [V]; "Find a location that's comfortable, private, and appropriate" [V]; and "One question that may be used as a good starter for interviews: 'What are you able to tell me about your experience?'" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews", sidebar).

The guide gives "words of caution when conducting interviews with employees that just lived through an unexpected outcome or tragedy" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). Where possible, the team asks the supervisor whether any employees are having a hard time with what occurred [AP]. "Be mindful of what information is needed for the FLA team's purposes of learning and what might be damaging to recall that won't significantly add to the learning or sensemaking" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). The guide sets a limit on how far an interview goes into traumatic memory: "don't deliberately take the interview into deeper recall experiences (leave that to the mental health professionals)" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). "However, sometimes as people are telling you what they saw and experienced, they may take you there anyway" [V], and for that case a specific *deflection-question* protocol is given: "If the person takes the interview to a difficult point of recall don't leave them there mentally. Be prepared with a few deflection questions to mentally 'walk the person away' from these vivid memories they are sharing with you" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). The worked examples are unusually concrete — the interviewer redirects from a witness's account of an engine going over a road edge to "take me back to that morning when you guys were at the engine bay, what time did your duty day start? What's a normal day look like for you guys?" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). The justification: "Deflection questions use inquiry to ask the witness about something that went right or something they know very well and are comfortable talking about. It helps pull their recall memory away from the site of the tragedy as they talk about this new line of inquiry" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). Nothing in the protocol steers the interview back to the memory afterwards; deeper recall is left to mental health professionals [AP] (Part 6, "Interviews"). The guide closes the caution with support: "it is important that people understand they can have access to mental health professionals and make sure they have the information they need to contact them. This includes the members of the FLA team themselves" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews").

Before interviews begin, the facilitator coaches interviewers on the interview guidance in Part 6 and Handout B [AP] (Part 6, "Interviews"); "The FLA facilitator should also remind the interviewers to collect quotes from the interviewees" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). The guide also instructs interviewers to "battle bias (see Handout C FLA 'Watch Outs')" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews") and to "focus on their objective to be able to describe how the people involved developed their understanding of the situation and made sense of their choices at the time and in context" [V] (Part 6, "Interviews"). Daily team debriefs are recommended.

A boxed commitment sits in the interview section: "No Signed Witness Statements: An FLA Commitment" (Part 6, "Interviews"). "Very often people involved in a traumatic event remember things that never actually happened and cannot recall key events that they were directly involved with. This is what happens to normal and honest people. We expect and intend for participants involved in the event to learn what actually happened along with the FLA team" [V]. The facilitated dialogue "is when the participants and witnesses all share their contrasting memories together with other information gathered by the team. This session is often punctuated by moments of shock and surprise as participants compare their memories with others" [V]. "Written, signed witness statements and recorded interviews may interfere with recreating the best account of what happened. Consequently, FLA Teams never collect written witness statements or record interviews. We don't want participants to feel like that have to maintain or defend early perspectives of what they think happened" [V] (Part 6, "No Signed Witness Statements: An FLA Commitment").

### Principles and Agreements for the Group Dialogue

The ten "Principles and Agreements for All Involved in the Facilitation" (Part 6, "Principles and Agreements for All Involved in the Facilitation") are the procedural commitment for the group dialogue session, given verbatim where load-bearing:

> "1. We have clear agreement with the Delegating Official that no administrative actions, (that is, disciplinary actions such as letters of caution, stand-downs, and forced re-trainings) may result from anything learned through the FLA process. If there is any question about this, stop and clear up confusion.
> 2. Respectful discussion is the rule; it can be emotional but it must remain respectful.
> 3. Learning for future events is more important than assessing past blame.
> 4. Be willing to be vulnerable. This discussion is not to find who 'caused' the accident. We are here only to share what each individual has learned from the incident and then see if we can turn that into collective learning.
> 5. The FLA team is not here to 'fix' a problem. This is only about taking advantage of an opportunity to learn. If anyone would rather use this session to prove someone else was wrong, they are invited to leave.
> 6. We all make mistakes—it's inevitable; it's the human condition. It's okay to openly discuss these occurrences.
> 7. Almost all human actions and decisions are intuitive responses to circumstances largely based on past experiences. It is extremely rare that our people are actually careless, meaning that they didn't care if the outcome was or was not as intended.
> 8. Accidents are almost always the result of rare combinations of normal performance variability and chance combinations of unlikely events.
> 9. Safety is never an absolute.
> 10. Within this dialogue, safety should be thought of, and referred to, as the reasonableness of risk. It is a feeling about which two experienced, competent professionals can disagree—and both be right!" [V] (Part 6, "Principles and Agreements for All Involved in the Facilitation").

### Participants and agenda for the group dialogue

Who attends depends on the event: "An experienced FLA facilitator is one most qualified to know who should and shouldn't be present" [V] (Part 6, "Participants"). "Typically, participants include everyone directly involved in the event including permittees, outfitters, cooperators, etc." [V] (Part 6, "Participants"). Depending on the situation, supporting FLA team members, supervisors of the people involved, project planners, project leaders and trainee facilitators may be included [AP] (Part 6, "Participants"). The guide flags the effect of seniority in the room: "When project leaders, supervisors, and Delegating Officials are involved in the dialogue the discussions often become broader in scope with organizational and interdepartmental topics included. In some cases, it may be more productive to conduct the discussion without these high-level members present. As a general rule, supervisors should not be present unless they were directly involved in the event" [V] (Part 6, "Participants"). The team leader and facilitator confer about, and control, who is present based on what they learned from the interviews; "Don't be afraid to ask the participants themselves who should be involved" [V] (Part 6, "Participants"). Leaders kept out of the dialogue are still interviewed: "Do interview project leaders, supervisors, Delegating Officials because they are participants in the decision. Their perspective on risk and how it may differ from participants is important for the FLA team to explore" [V] (Part 6, "Participants").

The agenda for the dialogue session is deliberately loose: "Only a general agenda is necessary. It should not constrain the flow of the discussion. Experienced facilitators have learned to ensure there is more than enough time available; dialogues often go for several hours or longer" [V] (Part 6, "Agenda for the Dialogue Session"). "Plan for the amount of time you think you'll need then make contingency plans in case the dialogue needs to go twice as long" [V] (Part 6, "Agenda for the Dialogue Session"). The opening is procedural: "Make sure to take a few minutes to explain the FLA process and discuss the principles and agreements above. Also, discuss the nature of the learning product that will document the learning" [V] (Part 6, "Agenda for the Dialogue Session").

### Facilitation moves

Specific facilitator moves recommended (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session"):

- **Location, location, location.** "It is basically the 'stage' for the FLA performance. The best location is almost always the field where the incident occurred" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session"). If field is not available, "don't just accept the 'available conference room.'"
- **You are not your point of view.** Open with a story where a smart person was absolutely convinced things were one way and turned out wrong; "the goal is to get people to feel that they don't have to defend their perspective" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session"). "Get agreement with your audience upfront that nobody's credibility is on the line" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session").
- **Invite uncertainty.** "Dare people to suspend any certainty they have in what happened and challenge them to anticipate (and even imagine) that over the next hour or two, they will be surprised by what they didn't know" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session").
- **Exploit points of departure.** "Points of departure, refers to the moments of inconsistency that occur in our accounts of the event that reflect the different perspectives that members hold. The idea is not to validate one story over the other but to reveal when these discrepancies occur so that all involved have a chance to see from another's perspective" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session"). A boxed warning beside it: "FEAR THE FUSION. NOT THE CONFUSION. When everyone is in agreement, you either didn't need to lead the facilitated group analysis (everyone is in agreement) or you haven't revealed points of departure or they don't want to talk about it" [V] (Part 6, box).
- **Encourage sensemaking.** Facilitation "closely resembles a group interview. The goal of the interviews is to obtain information from participants" [V]; by contrast, "The goal of the group dialogue session is to encourage sensemaking through dialogue to achieve a better understanding of the multiple perspectives of the participants" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session").
- **Listen for the silent voice.** "Many people, even some extroverts, do not feel comfortable speaking up in a group of peers. Some great thinkers don't feel confident in their ability to think on their feet, developing coherent arguments while talking at the same time. The facilitator needs be attentive these quiet participants and work them into the dialogue. Don't allow a self-directed dialogue to continue very long unless everyone is participating" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session").

Sand tables, Google Earth, and ArcMap are named as physical/digital aids that help reconstruct what people perceived at the time (Part 6, "Sand Tables, Google Earth, and ArcMap").

Three boxed items in Part 6 bear on the dialogue. "The specific details of interviews and deliberations must never be shared with anyone outside of the FLA Team, including the Delegating Official" [V] (Part 6, box beside "Principles and Agreements"). Isaacs's *Dialogue and the Art of Thinking Together* is "Strongly Recommended Reading for all FLA Facilitators" [V] [BT] (Part 6, box). "Pictures Are Precious": "FLA teams need to be proactive, even assertive in asking for pictures or video. Not only do pictures add much visual appeal to FLA reports, but they also contain valuable information, like time stamps, GPS coordinates and other important metadata" [V] (Part 6, "Pictures Are Precious"). A closing box adds that "There isn't a recipe card for conducting or 'producing' an FLA. It is up to the Team and the Delegating Official which story (there are always many) you chose to share and how you share it" [V]; the 2022 FLA "A Conversation on Partnerships, Risk and Safety" chose a story about the agency culture, structure and systems around the death of a youth volunteer [AE] (Part 6, box).

## Part VI: The complex FLA — Lessons Learned Analysis and the Five Hows (Part 7)

The Lessons Learned Analysis is the dialogue tool that distinguishes a complex FLA from a basic one. The opening epigram is a Dekker & Pruchnicki quote: "Actions that are interpreted as 'bad decisions' after an adverse event are, at the same time actions that seem reasonable – or people would not have taken them" [V] [BT] (Part 7, "The Lessons Learned Analysis", quoting Dekker & Pruchnicki 2013). The FLA team's stance follows: it "does not see wrongdoing, but rather tries to understand how people can see their actions as being right" [V] [BT] (Part 7, "The Lessons Learned Analysis", quoting Dekker & Pruchnicki).

"A Lesson Learned Analysis is a confidential team dialogue... The task is for the team to achieve the same level situational awareness, belief, and expectation that was held by those involved in the accident - which they had before the accident. The end-state is the insight generated from the dialogue itself. Consensus is not the goal. Tension between individual team member's perspectives is valuable" [V] (Part 7, "The Lessons Learned Analysis"). A pull quote from NAFRI's Learning from Unintended Outcomes Workshop names the test of success: "A Lessons Learned Analysis is not about explaining why those involved in the accident made their decisions. Rather, it about understanding the conditions surrounding the event so thoroughly that team members begin to believe that they themselves would have made exactly the same decisions! This is the defining moment of clarity. The team has gained the wisdom of knowing that similar conditions in the future will again lead to similar decisions and outcomes" [V] [BT] (Part 7, pull quote; "it about" as printed).

The *Five Hows* is the framing tool for the Lessons Learned Analysis. The guide presents the Five Hows as questions to be applied to each key action or decision in the event, with the explicit instruction that "You may find some of these 'hows' do not apply and some will be redundant. Use those that are helpful and don't waste time trying to cook-book the process" [V] (Part 7, "The Five Hows – A Sensemaking Tool"). The intent is to "explore how and why the decisions and actions that seemed wrong in hindsight were actually valid or at least legitimate in context at the time" [V] (Part 7, "The Five Hows – A Sensemaking Tool"). The graphic itself (read in the converted text and checked against a render of PDF p. 46) sets one stem, "How it made sense at the time of - and leading up to - the incident to ..." [V], at the centre of five completions: "...expect what they expected." "... ignore a risk that (in hindsight) seems so obvious." "... see things the way they were seen in their eyes." "... forgo an available hazard mitigation." "...shortcut a standard procedure or process." [V] (Part 7, "The Five Hows – A Sensemaking Tool", graphic). The five sit in a ring around the stem, so the order given here is the converted text's, not a sequence the source sets. A boxed tip beside it: "Keep the focus on the players involved in the incident. The focus is NOT 'how' it makes sense to the FLA team, but rather 'how' it made sense to those involved" [V] (Part 7, box).

The Lessons Learned Analysis procedure (Part 7, "A Process for conducting a Lessons Learned Analysis") is given as seven steps:

1. Gather the FLA team together in a secure, private meeting room.
2. Post the quotes and key bits of information from the interviews on flip chart paper and sticky notes, highlighting what participants learned for themselves and what they want management or fellow employees to learn.
3. Discuss the useful and interesting quotes — surprising, troubling, or hard-to-empathise-with statements or actions.
4. Identify interesting, odd, or disturbing lessons learned. For each, discuss the beliefs, perceptions, expectations, and paradigms held before the experience that in hindsight turned out wrong, inaccurate, misleading, or deceptive.
5. Identify and discuss the "key decisions" or "key actions" that flowed from those beliefs, perceptions, expectations, and paradigms.
6. Agree as a team on the most important key decisions or actions; for each, deliberate on the Five Hows in dialogue.
7. From this dialogue, write up the Lesson Learned Analysis explaining the sensemaking that occurred before and during the event and why, in context, the actions and decisions made sense.

"A successful Lessons Learned Analysis results in the team being less judgmental of the participants actions" [V] (Part 7, "The Lessons Learned Analysis"). "Most often, the Lessons Learned Analysis will reveal that multiple improbable events were necessary for the accident to occur" [V] (Part 7, "The Lessons Learned Analysis").

A boxed "Leader's Intent for a Complex FLA" sets the bar for the complex product: "A Complex FLA is successful if it describes what happed and shows how the decision and choices made by the people involved made sense leading up to the event. The FLA should include enough information about the context of the event such that the reader (or listener) can literally feel some of the surprise that the actors in the event felt at the time" [V]; "The analysis section should daylight the important workplace and human performance conditions that were influential in sensemaking at the time. It should also display the Gap between work as imagined by the administrators as compared to actual work accomplished by employees" [V]; and the product "should be in a format conducive to widespread agency learning" [V] (Part 7, "Leader's Intent for a Complex FLA"; "happed" as printed). A captioned example notes an FLA that "guides the reader into the 'boots' of the people who experienced this event by asking a series of questions to discuss key decisions and actions" [V] [AE] (Part 7, caption).

## Part VII: Storytelling — the FLA's primary learning artefact (Part 8)

"In an FLA, 'the story' should not be confused with fiction or an enhancement of facts. An FLA's story is a factual description of what occurred" [V] (Part 8, "Why FLA Storytelling?"). The cognitive justification: "Cognitive scientists have shown that humans make sense of, and remember, 'facts' by attaching them to narratives (i.e., stories) that give them context and a sensory or emotional association. If given a listing of findings with no story as context, our minds are prone to give these findings relevance by either creating a story, or by associating them with a story that is already within our memory. In other words, the lack of the story behind the 'facts' will actually lead to a distortion of the facts within our minds" [V] (Part 8, "Why FLA Storytelling?").

The guide emphasises perspective-respecting storytelling: "It is inevitable in any complex event that the people involved in the accident will have different perspectives and memories of what happened, and how, and why. Often the facilitated dialogue session will reconcile disparate stories. Occasionally however there will remain very different accounts of what happened. Don't see this as somebody being right and somebody being wrong" [V] (Part 8, "Different Perspectives"). The footnoted Dekker, Cilliers, Hofmeyr 2011 paper on *The Complexity of Failure* is cited verbatim: "respect otherness, difference in accounts about what happened as a value in itself. Diversity of narrative can be seen as an enormous source of resilience in complex system not as weakness. The more angles the more there can be to learn" [V] [BT] (Part 8, "Different Perspectives", quoting Dekker, Cilliers, Hofmeyr, *Safety Science* 49 (2011), p. 944).

The named storytelling craft elements (Part 8, "Storytelling Basics: tips for creative nonfiction storytellers") are given as a list; separately, Handout E attributes its three "storytelling critical elements (empathy pathways)" to Lisa Cron's *Wired for Story* [BT] (Handout E, "Tips for Facilitated Learning Analysis Storytelling", footnote 13):

- **Set up main character(s) without identifying information.** Tell us who these people are: their experiences, backgrounds, limited personal family backgrounds, physical traits — enough for readers to relate.
- **Set up the place.** "The fact that it was hot or cold, steep or flat, dusty or damp, may have no relevance to the actual event but these sensory details are necessary if we are to vicariously join the characters in their experience" [V] (Part 8, "Storytelling Basics").
- **Connect main characters with the place** — backstory, environment, how the characters arrived at the moment.
- **Share the character's internal voice** — what they want to achieve and why; differences between personal goals and public/outer goals; differences between what they want to do and what they are expected to do.
- **Challenges and obstacles or conflict** — "There are trade-offs between efficiency and thoroughness. There are always goal conflicts. Tell the reader what these are for the person" [V] (Part 8, "Storytelling Basics").
- **Sensemaking and decision making.** "These decisions must have seemed reasonable at the time given the conditions the character understood at the time. This does not mean that the storyteller is defending the decisions; rather, they are only relating how decisions made sense at the time" [V] (Part 8, "Storytelling Basics").

The *Readback* process (Part 8, "Validating Stories through the Readback process") gives all key participants the chance to hear the finalised learning product story read aloud by the FLA Team and to correct or clarify important details: "All of the key individuals involved with the accident should have an opportunity to hear the finalized FLA learning product's story read out loud by the FLA Team. They should be requested to correct or clarify important details and ensure that their lessons learned are captured correctly. Remember this is their story, not yours" [V] (Part 8, "Validating Stories through the Readback process"). "Even emotional or controversial comments can be powerful points of learning—providing they are captured appropriately in the context in which they were offered" [V] (Part 8, "Validating Stories through the Readback process"). Discrepancies that are the team's mistakes are resolved through follow-up interviews; discrepancies that come from multiple perspectives or different memories are captured in the learning product, in language that is neither judgmental nor shaped by hindsight bias [AP] (Part 8, "Validating Stories through the Readback process"). The guide recommends the readback occur in two phases — first to those directly involved, then to other participants, supervisors, and administrators. If people are shown hard copies of the learning product, all copies should be collected afterward to prevent contradictory copies from circulating. Bringing everyone together for story validation in a facilitated group can sometimes be appropriate, but "Use caution with this approach, as strong supervisors may suppress the voices of those who have different perspectives" [V] (Part 8, "Validating Stories through the Readback process"). Part 8 shows the craft with the opening lines of the Meadow Creek APA, a complex FLA: "CRRRAAACK! The unmistakable sound of a tree's holding wood popping ricocheted off the steep canyon walls early that July 5th afternoon" [V] [AE] (Part 8, sidebar). It closes on a Fire Operations Risk Management Council pull quote: "Usually what we find is that our workplace systems, protocols and rules are designed to accommodate optimal employees – not actual employees" [V] (Part 8, pull quote).

## Part VIII: Final FLA considerations and termination (Part 9)

The "Avoid Counterfactual Arguments" instruction is named explicitly: "FLA teams must guard against making counterfactual arguments such as: 'If this person had done X, then the outcome would have been Y and the accident would not have occurred.' The FLA is only useful when it learns why people did what they actually did (why it made sense to them at the time), rather than why they did not do something that — in hindsight — others might think they should have" [V] (Part 9, "Avoid Counterfactual Arguments").

The *Display Misalignments* step is the work-as-imagined / work-as-done diagnostic explicitly named: "Once the FLA team understands how the accident participants made sense of their environment, the team should contrast this understanding with how administrators thought employees would (or should) make sense of the environment. Illuminating the gap between work as imagined by administrators and work as actually accomplished will illuminate substantial and critical organizational vulnerabilities" [V] (Part 9, "Display Misalignments Between Different Aspects or Roles within the Organization").

Part 9's "Readbacks" section sets the timing: "As soon as a draft is available, the FLA team should ask those involved in the event to review it before anyone outside the team or the interviewed participants sees it" [V]; reading the product aloud is the recommended method, and distributing draft copies is not recommended [AP] (Part 9, "Readbacks"). On learning products, a pull quote from Dr. Jennifer Ziegler: "The objective is not the library; the objective is to create a movement using this new practice" [V] [BT] (Part 9, "FLA Learning Products", pull quote).

A boxed section covers a delegation that asks for cause: "If the delegation requires the FLA team to find cause, determine cause, or identify causal factors in the report, the team should define the word 'cause' within the report as 'The team's judgment of the conditions that describe the nature of the accident' including:" [V] "Conditions that create tension between production and protection; and," "Conditions that collectively permit the chance conjunctions of local triggers and active failures to breach all the barriers and safeguards" [V] [BT] (Part 9, "If the Delegation Requires You to Determine 'Cause'", "Adapted from The Human Condition by James Reason" as the source credits it).

A boxed "Privacy - A General Rule" governs names in the product: "Facilitated Learning Analysis reports typically avoid using people's names and only refer to gender if it is relevant to the incident or meaningful to the story" [V]. One acceptable technique "is to use fictitious, gender-neutral names such as Terry, Tracy, Lynn, Leslie, etc." [V], making sure the reader knows they are fictitious and why; on wildland fires a person's ICS position can be given ("DIVS A" or a fictitious "DIVS Smith") for organisational and command context [AP] (Part 9, "Privacy - A General Rule").

### Termination criterion: reckless and willful disregard

"During the course of the FLA process, though highly unlikely, it could be discovered that an agency employee acted with a reckless and willful disregard for human safety or committed a serious criminal act" [V] (Part 9, "Serious Crimes or Reckless and Willful Disregard for Human Safety"). In such cases, "the event may no longer be appropriate for a 'safety investigation' (FLA). Why? Because the event is no longer considered an 'accident.'" [V] (Part 9, "Serious Crimes or Reckless and Willful Disregard for Human Safety"). The FLA team leader writes a memo to the Delegating Official terminating the FLA and recommending an administrative or law enforcement investigation; physical evidence is released to the Delegating Official; interview notes and other team products are given to the lead facilitator for confidential and secure storage; "team members must not discuss anything they learned during the FLA process with anyone" [V] (Part 9, "Serious Crimes or Reckless and Willful Disregard for Human Safety") apart from cooperation with external authorities outside agency control.

The reckless-and-willful threshold is defined in Appendix C: "A reckless and willful disregard for human safety is conduct that is intentional, unjustifiable, and occurred with the foreknowledge that the conduct was likely to result in serious harm, death, or injury to a human" [V] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?").
