"FLAs are for the vast majority of events in which good people, doing what they thought made sense at the time, ended up in an unexpected situation" [V] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?").

### Is an FLA the right tool? (Appendix C)

Appendix C gives the Delegating Official four questions to answer before choosing the tool; Part 5 has the Delegating Official and the FLA team review each item together at the in-brief (Part 5, "Clear Mutual Objectives"; Appendix C, "Questions for the Delegating Official").

- **Is litigation against an employee or the agency likely as a result of the accident?** "If the answer to this question is 'Yes,' the Delegating Official should consider a confidential administrative investigation. An FLA investigation is inappropriate under the threat of a criminal or civil action" [V] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?").
- **Is there evidence that an act of reckless and willful disregard for human safety directly contributed to the accident?** If yes, "the Delegating Official should consider an administrative or law enforcement investigation" [V]; if the team uncovers such an act, "the team may not be able to sustain the trust and confidence of other accident participants—knowing that disciplinary action is likely" [V] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?"). The threshold definition quoted above sits in this answer, along with the reason an FLA fits the ordinary case: "one of chief benefits of an FLA is to hold the agency accountable for designing safe systems and managing human reliability" [V]; "If an employee harms another employee intentionally, that employee is responsible and an FLA is likely the wrong response" [V] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?").
- **Is the Delegating Official committed to disseminating the lessons learned in a public report?** "The answer to this question must be 'Yes.'" [V] "Some information in the learning product may make you feel uncomfortable. This is exactly what is needed in a learning culture" [V]; members at all levels need to see leaders reflecting on their experiences and sharing what they learned from accidents and close calls [AP] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?").
- **Is the Delegating Official committed to "learning" rather than "punishing"?** "The answer to this question must be 'Yes.'" [V] "If punishment is intended, in whatever form, the FLA process should be dropped. The FLA's overriding purpose is always individual and organizational learning" [V] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?"). "The learning that will result from this constructive process will far outweigh any perceived benefit that might be derived from punishing individuals for making errors, mistakes, or violating rules" [V] (Appendix C, "Is an FLA the Right Tool?").

## Part IX: The Learning Review (Parts 10–11)

The Learning Review extends the FLA when the Delegating Official wants vetted recommendations and is willing to own them. The conceptual frame is analysis-vs-synthesis: "Analysis is the go-to method for gaining understanding in the western world. It involves breaking things down into components and then trying to figure out which component is broken. This has proven to be a very useful method, especially with respect to machines... The machine metaphor is not as widely applicable as our culture seems to give it credit for" [V] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"). "Life is an emergent property that cannot be fully examined through analysis" [V] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"). "Synthesis is the process of trying to understand how emergent properties come to be. It is a study of how things are put together (rather than taken apart)" [V] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"). The LR "incorporates both analysis and synthesis through sensemaking" [V] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?").

The LR's diagnostic questions: "Are our policies keeping up with a changing system of work?" "Is our organization sending mixed messages to field-going personnel?" "Do our employees face goal conflicts of which management is unaware?" [V] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"). Some FLA data deserves direct analysis — a failed aircraft engine sent to the manufacturer for teardown, for example, with deeper collaboration between manufacturer and agency during the LR [AE] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"). "The Learning Review may include the addition of academic and professional subject-matter experts as an option to support the Learning Review process. Humans are not like machines. They learn and adapt and are never fully predictable" [V] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?"). "There are events or outcomes that might give a team or agency administer pause and want to dig deeper than the FLA process provides" [V] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"; "administer" as printed).

### How a Learning Review is initiated and staffed

When the FLA concludes, a formal briefing with the Delegating Official decides whether to publish the FLA as a standalone product or to invest in a Learning Review to develop recommendations [AP] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"). "The Delegating Official needs to understand that the Learning Review process is a significant investment and requires a willingness on the part of the Delegating Official to convene and chair a Learning Review Board" [V] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"). "If the Delegating Official decides they want recommendations and they are willing to take ownership of any recommendations the board approves, then the Learning Review process is initiated through a request to the Risk Management Council (RMC)" [V]; the RMC appoints a Learning Review process coach, who works with the FLA team to capture the conditions and influences surfaced in the Lessons Learned Analysis, using a network of influences map or similar [AP] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"). The complex narrative and the map go to one or more focus groups "comprised of members of different communities of practice (e.g. line officers, engine crewmembers, hotshots, helitack crewmembers, wildland fire module crewmembers, sawyers, trail crew members, timber markers)" [V] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"). "The purpose of the focus group(s) is to identify what can be learned from the event. They are also given the opportunity to construct recommendations, or vet recommendations constructed by others to ensure the recommendations are feasible and will actually improve the work system design" [V] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"). "The team leader, in conjunction with the Delegating Official, has the option to recruit and employ outside perspectives such as academics or members of other communities (e.g. the military) that may provide unique subject matter for recommendations that lead to outside-the-box innovations and recommendations" [V] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"). Once the complex narrative, the network of influences map, a sensemaking document (the focus-group input) and the proposed recommendations are complete, a Learning Review Board is convened [AP] (Part 10, "An overview of the process"). A graphic, "A General outline for the Learning Review Process" [V], gives the sequence as boxes joined by arrows: the Delegating Official identifies need for recommendations; Learning Review process initiated; Network of Influences created; focus group(s) convene; focus group sensemaking; focus group generates or vets recommendations; Learning Review team generates document and/or products; Learning Review Board convened; Board approves learning products and recommendations; products sent to the RMC to be posted/shared; Safety Action Plan finalized [AP] (Part 10, graphic; order read from a render of PDF p. 59).

The RMC works with IOL to find the Learning Review Process Coach, and the LR team is a collaboration between the FLA Team Lead, the process coach and SMEs [AP] (Part 10, "Learning Review Team Composition"). "Any recommendations developed by the Learning Review team will be vetted through the communities of practice affected by the recommendation" [V]; once the communities of practice have vetted and agreed to them, the team prepares a presentation for the Learning Review Board [AP] (Part 10, "Learning Review Team Composition").

For mechanical, ergonomic, and structural failures, the LR explicitly admits engineering-based analysis: "'analysis' is applicable only to objective information and is conducted to assess mechanical, ergonomic, and structural failures. It follows an engineering-based model, which is dedicated to problem-solving using quantitative data" [V] (Part 10, "How the learning review process examines mechanical, ergonomic and structural failures"). The output is often a *barrier* (tangible — physical or mechanical — or intangible — rules, regulations, policies, procedures), which either prevents an incident or mitigates its results, as a seatbelt lessens severity without preventing the crash [AE]. "Barriers can also make systems and work more complicated, so their development and introduction should be vetted through those closest to the work that they will affect" [V] (Part 10, "How the learning review process examines mechanical, ergonomic and structural failures"). "Barriers have been shown to be effective in simple and complicated systems. Therefore, barriers may be appropriate in cases where analysis can successfully provide answers to problems. Complex systems are non-linear by definition, and barriers have proven to be less effective in social (complex) situations" [V] (Part 10, "How the learning review process examines mechanical, ergonomic and structural failures"). "The Learning Review process is predicated on the assumption that sensemaking and identification of influences within the system will be a much more effective means of improving accident rates" [V] (Part 10, "How the learning review process examines mechanical, ergonomic and structural failures"). Sidney Dekker's *The Field Guide to Understanding Human Error* (Ashgate 2014) is cited verbatim for the sensemaking frame: "in complex situations, people must act based on uncertain, incomplete, and sometimes even contradictory information" [V] [BT] (Part 10, "The learning review process", footnote 8). The LR team's job is to make visible the interactions, conditions and circumstances that shaped a person's assessments and actions [AP] (Part 10, "The learning review process"). The steps that follow are "merely an attempt to provide LR teams with a jumping off point. Ultimately, the data should drive the process and LR teams should adjust/develop the LR process to meet the needs of the incident" [V] (Part 10, "The learning review process").

- **1. Building the Learning Review team.** A Learning Review team forms either when the Delegating Official wants recommendations from the start (the FLA's process coach, familiar with both processes, then leads the focus groups) or after a complex FLA has concluded (if the FLA process coach is not familiar with a Learning Review, a Learning Review process coach joins the FLA process coach and team) [AP]. "At a minimum, the LR team should be composed of members of the FLA team and a process coach" [V]. The focus group is the design response to a known weakness: "In the past we relied on investigation team members to draw conclusions based on the information they acquired during the investigation. This approach did not recognize the limitations of such a small team" [V]; "Focus groups are a recognized way of including new ideas, viewpoints, and knowledge from sources outside the team" [V] (Part 10, "1. Building the Learning Review Team").
- **2. Preparing to hold the first focus group.** The team reviews the narrative and the Network of Influences map and decides which SMEs and academic specialists might help [AP]. "There is no recipe for establishing focus groups that applies to all events" [V]; multiple focus groups may be needed, for example organisational leadership, senior fire leaders or technical specialists [AP]. "Focus group feedback helps us concentrate on understanding the applicability of conditions to the actual (real) world of how work is accomplished" [V] (Part 10, "2. Preparing to Hold the First Focus Group"). Placing the event's actions and decisions in the context of the work system means "Recommendations will therefore become relevant to the entire work system rather than limited to accident-specific conditions, which may never occur again" [V] (Part 10, "2. Preparing to Hold the First Focus Group").
- **3. Using academic review.** "Academic specialists can add yet another lens or perspective that will enhance the ability to be self-reflective as an organization and thereby learn from the event" [V]; giving the academics the narrative and the enhanced network of influences map "will provide a more neutral (outside) view of organizational operations" [V] (Part 10, "3. Using Academic Review").

### The Learning Review Board (Part 11)

"The culmination of the accident review process is the Learning Review Board. A Learning Review Board will be conducted anytime the Delegating Official wants formal recommendations as an outcome of the accident review process" [V] (Part 11, "Learning Review Board"). Outside a Coordinated Response Protocol response, the Delegating Official has broad latitude in creating the board [AP]. "Successful Learning Review Boards encompass a broad range of experience and diverse backgrounds as a means of shedding light on potential problems with proposed recommendations" [V]; they "can also be viewed as a structured means of fostering conversations between the Delegating Official and his or her staff" [V] (Part 11, "Learning Review Board"). A district ranger's board would likely be trusted members of their staff, a forest supervisor's their Forest Leadership Team, with outside expertise brought in where needed [AP]; "The board is chaired by the Delegating Official or their designee" [V] (Part 11, "Learning Review Board"). The board receives the complex narrative, the network of influences map and the focus groups' proposed recommendations, and gives input and feedback [AP]. Once it approves them, the learning products go to a member of the Risk Management Council to be posted, "and the recommendations are organized into a Safety Action Plan that the Delegating Official takes ownership of and is responsible for following up on to ensure the recommendations are carried out and implemented. The Safety Action Plan describes the recommendation(s), assigns each to a person or body to be responsible for carrying it out, and provides a deadline of when each is to be accomplished" [V] (Part 11, "Learning Review Board").

Recommendations "should enhance the system in terms of prevention, resilience, or corrections/revisions to existing rules, regulations, policies, or procedures" [V] (Part 11, "Recommendations"). "It is required that recommendations be circulated through representatives of the community of practice (commonly through focus groups) and the Risk Management Council prior to the Learning Review Board. The result of this process should be to enhance recommendations to ensure they are reasonable and are consistent with existing research" [V] (Part 11, "Recommendations"). The LRB then creates the *Safety Action Plan*: "The SAP will designate who is responsible for completing the recommendation(s). Those responsible for the completion of an action item listed on the SAP should be consulted prior to committing any resource to an action item or recommendation. This is designed to avoid unnecessary requests for extensions" [V] (Part 11, "Recommendations").

At least two learning products are produced, because people in the field manage risk in real time with less influence over rules and policy than senior leaders, who "must be prepared with information so that they can exert that influence in the most productive manner" [V] (Part 11, "Learning Review Products"). The Learning Review Product Summary Table sets the development, recommendation-vetting, and action expectations for each product; organisational recommendations are vetted through the LR Process Coach, the FLA Team Leader and especially the communities of practice they affect, before submission to the board [AP] (Part 11, "Learning Review Product Summary Table"). "Organizational and field learning should be recognized as a legitimate 'corrective action' following an event" [V]; "field-learning products may be the only recommendation required to meet the goal of prevention through learning" [V] (Part 11, "Organizational and Field Learning").

- **Organizational Learning Product** — "directed to answer the specific needs of the organization, in terms of understanding the organizational, structural, systemic, and cultural contributors to the event" [V]. Designed for policy-makers and higher levels. "Products should help these individuals to understand the gap between 'work as imagined' and 'work as performed.'" [V] (Part 11, "Organizational Learning Product"). "Organizational interventions should avoid quick fixes or knee-jerk reactions; they should be well thought out and vetted through the community of practice before recommendations are made to the Learning Review Board" [V] (Part 11, "Organizational Learning Product"). The systemic weaknesses it describes may include espoused values versus values in practice, the value of performance diversity and adaptation, how accountability functioned before the event, structural incongruities in rules and procedures, role confusion, practical drift, communication up, down and across the organisation, system design (tools, equipment, tasks, workload, capacity), and the physical environment [AP] (Part 11, "Organizational Learning Product").
- **Field Learning Product** — designed for district or field-office employees. "This does not mean that the narrative should be oversimplified or presented from a single point of view" [V]; "Complex interactions should be explored from all available perspectives, and our personnel should be encouraged to draw their own conclusions" [V] (Part 11, "Field Learning Product"). "Lessons should be emphasized emotively through dialogue, experientially through simulation, or by engaging the readers in personal reflection regarding their own experiences" [V] (Part 11, "Field Learning Product"). "The team should not feel limited to conventional written reports; they should consider creative tools such as high-tech graphics and multimedia presentations" [V] (Part 11, "Field Learning Product"). "This product should inspire rich dialogue by asking the reader/viewer to reflect and make sense of the event" [V], for example with "What part of this narrative can you relate to and how might this change the way you view this type of scenario?" [V] (Part 11, "Field Learning Product").

Before the board, the final-draft learning product goes through a Freedom of Information Act review so that the product delivered to the LRB is final and releasable once approved; "The goal is to create an un-redacted learning product to the LRB" [V] (Part 11, "Freedom of Information Act Review (FOIA)"). Where a regulator with agency oversight requires a causal statement, "this causal statement will be crafted at the end of the Learning Review" [V], drafted jointly by a Risk Management Council representative, the Learning Review Process Coach, the FLA Team Leader, the Regional Occupational Health and Safety Manager, a community-of-practice representative, and team members and specialists as required [AP] (Part 11, "Report to Regulator").

## Part X: Bias and watch-outs (Handout C, Handout D, Appendix B)

Handout C names four biases plus one habit of thought as the FLA team's recurring watch-outs (Handout C, "FLA 'Watch outs'"). The body text identifies hindsight bias explicitly: "Human memory connects images and facts to build a coherent mental story that makes sense in the light of the now known outcome. This is not a conscious process. 'Sensemaking' (see definition in glossary) does not stop after the accident. It is common to interview a firefighter involved in an accident and find their language packed with things they wished they had done differently. Then, in the subsequent weeks, this person's language changes to the certainty of what other people should have done" [V] (Handout C, "FLA 'Watch outs'"). The recommended counter-move is to interview as soon as possible and "help keep them focused on telling the story solely from their perspective" [V] (Handout C, "FLA 'Watch outs'"). The handout's graphic names the four biases and the way of thinking (Handout C, graphic, PDF pp. 87–88): confirmation bias, the fundamental attribution error, outcome bias, hindsight bias, and counterfactual thinking. Only two of the five boxes are text in the PDF; the other three are drawn as graphics, so neither the converted text nor `pdftotext` holds them, and they are described here from a render and a tesseract OCR of the pages [AP]:

- **Confirmation bias:** the tendency to attend selectively to what confirms one's beliefs (after an accident, looking for evidence for what one thinks happened) and to ignore or undervalue what contradicts them [AP] (Handout C, graphic, from OCR).
- **Fundamental attribution error:** "People have an extremely hard time noticing the influence of context. It feels much more natural to focus on people's personalities to account for their behavior rather than on influencing conditions" [V]; the example is assuming that someone who bumps into you is "an inconsiderate jerk" [V] when, "if you were in their shoes—you probably would have behaved the same way" [V] (Handout C, graphic).
- **Outcome bias:** evaluating a decision or action by its outcome rather than by the conditions that influenced it, which leads to judging actions and decisions as good or bad, right or wrong [AP] (Handout C, graphic, from OCR).
- **Hindsight bias:** the knew-it-all-along effect, believing a past event was easier to predict than it was; the team should reason together about how the same decisions could have led to the outcome the participants expected, and how different initiatives could have led to the same unexpected outcome [AP] (Handout C, graphic, from OCR).
- **Counterfactual thinking:** "Counterfactual means 'contrary to the facts.' Engaging in counterfactual thinking presumes that you can predict the future. What team members may think should have happened are the most seductive counterfactuals and they will blind the team from understanding the event in context" [V]; examples include "If only the firefighter had . . ." "The crew leader failed to . . . " "The supervisor should have . . ." [V] (Handout C, graphic).

"Remember, if the person involved in the accident had known what the results would be, they probably would have taken a different action. But the future hadn't happened yet, and they couldn't have known the outcome" [V] (Handout C, "FLA 'Watch outs'").

The Roese & Vohs 2012 *Perspectives on Psychological Science* paper on hindsight bias is named in Recommended Reading [BT] (Recommended Reading, "Accident, Safety and Human Performance").

Handout D presents two dialogue styles for facilitated group dialogue: AAR-type questions and *Organizing for High Reliability*-type questions, drawn from Weick and Sutcliffe's High Reliability Organisations work [BT] (Handout D, "Two Different Styles for Dialogue Focused Questions"). "The five hallmarks of High Reliability Organizations (HRO) can also be used to help structure or frame a facilitated dialogue" [V] (Handout D, "Two Different Styles for Dialogue Focused Questions"); the Glossary names the five as "preoccupation with failure, reluctance to oversimplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience and deference to expertise" [V] [BT] (Glossary, "High Reliability Organization", attributed in the source to Weick and Sutcliffe). The guide limits when to use them: "Generally, these questions should be reserved for cases in which the people who were involved with the incident are already familiar with the HRO traits and understand the principles" [V] (Handout D, "Two Different Styles for Dialogue Focused Questions"). The core of an HRO-based dialogue is the question "What did you (or we) learn from this event that will move us closer to actualizing each of these traits?" [V] (Handout D). The first style, AAR-type questions, is the default: "Dialogue facilitators most commonly use the well-known After-Action Review questions. These questions are designed to evoke discussion and escort participants to share their perspectives" [V], and "Notes from the Dialogue session will be very helpful when writing the FLA story and developing a learning product" [V] (Handout D, "After Action Review-Type Questions"). The six questions [V] (Handout D, "After Action Review-Type Questions"):

1. "What was planned? What was your leader's intent?"
2. "What information were you provided? What did you feel was missing? Why couldn't you get this?"
3. "What was the situation? What did you see? What were you aware of that you couldn't see?"
4. "What did you do? Why did you do it? What didn't you do? Why didn't you do it?"
5. "What was routine? What surprised you?"
6. "What did you learn? What might you do differently next time? What can we learn as an organization? What might we do differently?"

For the HRO style, the facilitator asks each participant what happened before the incident and what was learned about the organization afterwards, with regard to each trait [AP]. Example HRO-style questions named in the source (Handout D, "Two Different Styles for Dialogue Focused Questions"):

- "What were we sure that we do not want to misestimate? How well did we do? Did we do a pre-mortem? What were our trigger points and how effective were they?"
- "Where was our attention? How did we identify what was going on?"
- "What cues were we paying attention to in the environment? Where did we contain small errors before they had big consequences? What surprised us?"
- "Who did we listen to? Who did we not listen to?"
- "Was this a 'brutal audit'? What did we learn about our system, including brittle points where small errors had big consequences? Where do we need to build in more redundancy or more slack? How easily can we bounce back? What does this incident tell us about the environment we work in now?"

Appendix B's argument against causal factors is one of the guide's strongest position statements:

> "There is a deliberate effort in the FLA process to avoid labeling human errors, omissions or other actions (or non-actions) as 'causal.' Labeling these findings as 'cause' impedes our ability to explain or understand what was experienced in context before the accident. Constructing causal statements in complex systems inevitably degrades our ability to understand the complex nature of accidents, the role of chance, and nature of human performance functioning in dynamic environments." [V] (Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors").

> "Causal statements inevitably lack context because, for one, context is too complex; and two, because once context is explained you'll find cause becomes a conclusion that no longer follows from the premise (a non sequitur). Cause isn't something investigators 'find' or 'discover'; cause is always something we create by recreating the event showing how certain anomalies led to the accident." [V] (Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors").

> "Finally, causal statements tend to imply that safety is the responsibility of the people on the front lines facing the risks ... This impedes learning because it faults only one part of the system. However, safety is in the entire system. Practitioners at the 'sharp end' (those workers who directly confront the risks of the workplace) are inheritors of policies, training programs, tools, culture, incentives, etc., that are the responsibility of those managers and administrators at the 'blunt-end.'" [V] (Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors").

The source attributes this framing to the Hollnagel 2008 *Resilience Engineering Perspectives* reading: "Accidents are more accurately understood as unexpected combinations of normal performance variability (both human and system performance variability)" [V] [BT] (Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors", footnoted to Hollnagel 2008, p. 75).

## Part XI: Risk-as-feeling and the safety-vs-production tradeoff (Handout A)

Handout A condenses the guide's position on risk and safety into bullets (Handout A, "Understanding the Work Under a Just Culture"):

- "Risk is inherent in everything we do. Short of never doing anything, there is no way to avoid all risk or ever to be 100% safe" [V] (Handout A).
- "How employees (at any level) perceive, anticipate, interpret, and react to risk is systematically connected to conditions associated with the design, systems, features, and culture of the workplace" [V] (Handout A).
- Risk-as-construct, attributed to Paul Slovic (quoted via Kahneman's *Thinking Fast and Slow*, 2011, p. 141): "Risk does not exist 'out there,' independent of our minds and culture, waiting to be measured. Human beings have invented the concept of 'risk' to help them understand and cope with the dangers and the uncertainties of life. Although these dangers are real, there is no such thing as a 'real risk' or 'objective risk.'" [V] [BT] (Handout A, "Understanding the Work Under a Just Culture", quoting Slovic via Kahneman).
- "The best definition of 'safety' is: the reasonableness of risk. It is a feeling. It is not an absolute. It is personal and contextual and will vary between people even within identical situations" [V] (Handout A).
- "While safety is an essential business practice, our agency does not exist to be safe or to protect our employees. We exist to accomplish a taxpayer-funded mission as efficiently as possible — knowing that many activities we choose to perform are inherently hazardous" [V] (Handout A).
- "Essentially every risk mitigation (every safety precaution) carries some level of 'cost' to production or compromise to efficiency... Employees at all levels (administrators, safety advisors, system designers, and front-line employees) are continuously — and often subconsciously — estimating, balancing, optimizing, managing, and accepting these subtle and nuanced tradeoffs between safety and production" [V] (Handout A).
- "Our natural intuition (our common sense) is to let outcomes draw the line between success and failure and to base safety programs on outcomes. This is shortsighted and eventually dangerous... Risk Management is wholly concerned with managing risks, not outcomes. Risk management is counterintuitive" [V] (Handout A).

A boxed "PARADIGM CHECK POINT" beside the handout: "If some team members are new to the process, it may be helpful to pause and have a team discussion or even a full dialogue session around these points. Team members will have a hard time understanding the FLA process unless they understand these concepts" [V] (Handout A, box).

## Part XII: Lessons and Advice for FLA Teams (Appendix E)

Practitioner advice consolidated across years of FLA implementations (Appendix E, "Lessons and Advice for fla teams"):

- Don't forget the overall health and wellbeing of yourself and your team — pulse check. Make arrangements for work and personal life before taking an assignment.
- Take the time to build the Team and Align Team Values. "Make sure everyone reads the FLA guide" [V] (Appendix E). Plan for team-cohesion work to take at least a couple of hours. Use Handout A to drive a respectful dialogue point-by-point.
- Everyone on the team should be able to explain the FLA process in a succinct manner. Each member should think about their individual *why* for being on the team.
- Choose the Local Liaison Wisely and Put the Liaison to Work Quickly. Multiple liaisons may be needed (logistics, spokesperson, hospital, CISM, family, regional/state office, cooperator, agency rep, IMT).
- Utilise a process coach to provide an impartial view or advice for the team.
- Lay Out the Road Map and Adjust as Needed. "Don't just tell team members to 'trust the process'. People want know where they are and what is going to happen next and know they are making progress" [V] (Appendix E).
- Debrief with the Team Every Evening. The lead facilitator schedules end-of-day sharing.
- Stay Together. "Keep the team physically together until you have a solid draft. Letting people go home and trying to complete the learning product by emails and conference calls will inevitably add problematic delays" [V] (Appendix E).
- Don't Skimp on Peer Participation (the guide flags this as CRITICAL). "Ensure that peers are part of the team. The importance of having people on the team that are 'peers' to the people involved in the unintended outcome cannot be overstated. Don't try to save money or minimize the footprint of the team by cutting these positions" [V] (Appendix E).

A captioned photo notes that "The FLA process can be used in almost any type of unintended outcome, including aviation incidents such as the Davies Creek Ridge FLA in 2011" [V] [AE] (Appendix E, caption).

## Part XIII: Briefings for Delegating Officials (Appendix D)

Appendix D offers material for a Delegating Official preparing for a team's arrival and departure, or for a team learning what is expected; it "is not exhaustive but provided to share what has been learned over the years to be helpful for those involved in this process" [V] (Appendix D, "Briefings for Delegating Officials").

The **In Briefing Checklist** runs: schedule the in-brief (in person or virtual, sized to who needs to be there); introductions; a brief overview of the incident ("FLA team does not want an in-depth story" [V]); the leader's intent (expectations, desired schedule of updates, desired audience for the learning products, sensitivities about people, sites or media, other agencies or ongoing investigations, the best way to make contact, and a read-through of the Delegation of Authority with time for comments); logistics (team workplace, travel, food and lodging, printers); contacts (the assigned liaisons, and "Who is in the 'bullseye'? Thoughts on interviewees and least impactful time for those interviews" [V]); timeframes and budget (initial estimates, and timeframes for debriefing, the rough narrative, readbacks and publishing); scale of effort; union involvement; and thanking the team [AP] (Appendix D, "In Briefing Checklist").

**Debriefing the Delegating Official and leadership** comes once most information is gathered and a rough draft exists. "The intent of this meeting is not to read the draft of the FLA but to share an overview of the story, report about where the Team is at in the process and a chance to discuss the next steps" [V] (Appendix D, "Debriefing The Delegating Official and Leadership"). An example oral briefing, which teams "are encouraged to tailor this to meet their needs" [V], runs in eight steps, each with a worked example (Appendix D, "Debriefing The Delegating Official and Leadership"); the step wording is verbatim [V]:

1. "Thank the people who helped you get your work done."
2. "Briefly review the overall goals of the FLA." Example: "Provide individuals most directly involved in an event an opportunity to tell their stories. Capture and share practices that helped make the mission a success, and share lessons learned that might improve the probability of success in future incidents."
3. "Report out on who you interviewed and what information you gathered?"
4. "Preview the major parts of the story." Example: "Background, Narrative of the event, Lessons for sharing."
5. "Provide a very brief summation."
6. "Provide a preview of the lesson categories with enough information to illustrate them."
7. "Is there any information that might be useful for the Forest but will NOT be in the learning document." Example: "It may not have made a difference here, but we found that some of the IWI documents have broken links or old phone numbers."
8. "What are the next steps? What is a reasonable expectation for a timeline?" — "Be thoughtful about the time it takes to get feedback, who will be involved in the process, and how long that typically takes."

## Part XIV: Restorative Just Culture Checklist (Appendix F)

Appendix F is two pages held in the PDF as images (PDF pp. 77–78), credited to Professor Sidney Dekker (Griffith University, Delft University and Art of Work) and marked public domain [BT]. The converted text carries only the heading, so this section is read from a tesseract OCR of the page images checked against a render, and it paraphrases throughout: the check-verbatim tool can only verify quotations against the converted text (Appendix F, from OCR).

The checklist states that a restorative just culture aims to repair trust and relationships damaged after an incident and lets all parties discuss how they have been affected and decide together what should be done to repair the harm [AP]. It asks five sets of questions, each marked no or yes [AP] (Appendix F, "Restorative Just Culture Checklist", from OCR):

- **Acknowledged — who is hurt?** First victims (patients, passengers, colleagues, consumers, clients), second victims (the practitioners involved), the organisation (reputational or other harm) and the community (those who witnessed or were affected).
- **Explored — what do they need?** For example, information, access, restitution and reassurance of prevention for first victims; psychological first aid, compassion and reinstatement for second victims; information, leverage for change and reputational repair for the organisation; information and reassurance for the community.
- **Identified — whose obligation is it to meet the need?** Whether first victims are willing to tell their story and take part, whether second victims are willing to tell the truth, express remorse and contribute to learning, whether the organisation is willing to take part, has offered help and explored systemic fixes, and whether the community is willing to take part.
- **Ready to forgive?** Forgiveness as a process between people: confession, remorse, forgiveness.
- **Achieved the goals of restorative justice?** Moral engagement, emotional healing, reintegrating the practitioner, and organisational learning that explores and addresses systemic causes of harm.

The second page sets out the background. A restorative just culture asks who is hurt, what they need and whose obligation that is, with forward-looking accountability, where an account is something you tell and learn from; a retributive just culture asks what rule was broken, how bad the breach is and what the consequences should be, with backward-looking accountability, where an account is something you settle or pay [AP]. It lists reasons to avoid a retributive just culture: it can become a blunt HR or managerial instrument to get rid of people; it excludes the voices of first victims, colleagues and community; it is linked with hiding incidents; the more powerful people are, the more just they find it; and it does not identify systemic contributions, thus inviting repetition [AP]. It describes hurts, needs and obligations, forgiveness as a relational process that takes time, and the four goals; on reintegration it asks what firing someone fixes [AP] (Appendix F, "Background of Restorative Justice", from OCR).

## Part XV: Delegation of Authority templates (Appendices G and H)

Both templates carry the note that "Delegations of Authority should be negotiated between the team and the official. The material provided in this template is not mandatory" [V] (Appendix G; Appendix H).

The **basic FLA** template gives the Team Leader "the full authority of my office to execute and complete an FLA" [V], names a logistics coordinator and liaison and a coach, and expects the 72-hour (Preliminary Accident Briefing) report and the final report as soon as practicable [AP]. It records the Delegating Official's judgment that the event "does not warrant a complex FLA with a Lessons Learned Analysis" [V], and asks to be told of anything that would add significantly to its complexity [AP]. Its assurances: "I expect you to terminate this investigation if you uncover information that leads you to believe this accident resulted from a reckless and willful disregard for human safety. I respect that the information you collect from interviews will remain confidential even in this instance. I also agree that no punitive actions will be taken by the <insert agency here> against any employee as a result of information provided to any member of your team" [V], with participants told that actions by civil authorities or other agencies are outside the official's authority [AP]. The Team Leader's authority covers directing the analysis, managing confidentiality and evidence, adding and releasing personnel, funds and media releases [AP]. Optional directions include examining "specific conditions and influences (cultural, organizational, systemic as well as environmental) that may have affected the outcome" [V], "I am willing to hear the hard truths that may result from this examination" [V], and "If recommendations are discussed, a Learning Review will need to be implemented" [V] (Appendix G).

The **complex FLA** template adds the focus, "how the events leading up to this accident made sense at the time to those involved" [V], a mentor and coach for complex FLAs, and "I expect you to interview all participants in this event, including the Delegating official" [V]. Its authority list adds issuing Safety Alerts in coordination with the Regional Safety Manager, and its closing directions ask the Team Leader to give counsel verbally at the end and to consult the official in advance before adding a recommendation section, which would mean following the Learning Review process [AP] (Appendix H).

## Part XVI: Interviewing techniques (Handout B)

Handout B sets out "some basic principles interviewers should keep in mind" [V] (Handout B, "Interviewing Techniques"), in four groups:

- **Comfort.** "An interview should feel like sitting down to chat with someone but with the interviewer has the sole purpose to listen" [V]. "Remember the intent for the Interview: You are there to help capture their story" [V]. "Start with easy, friendly questions and work your way up to more difficult or sensitive information" [V]. "Remain neutral. Try not to agree or disagree with statements made, including when critical junctures are discussed in their story" [V] (Handout B, "Comfort").
- **Be curious.** "Never ask WHY; instead ask HOW or WHAT. Never ask why the interviewee made a key decision or action" [V]. "Ask how they came to make such and such a decision or, how they thought taking such and such action would improve the outcome" [V]. "The 'why' question puts people immediately on the defensive" [V]. "One way to get at the 'why' without putting folks on the defensive is to ask, 'What was going through your mind as that was occurring?'" [V] (Handout B, "Be Curious").
- **Listen.** "What you look for is what you find" [V], with a pointer to Handout C. "Preconceived notions, ideas or a prepared list of questions can cause you to steer the conversation and can have negative impacts on your interview" [V]. "Listen. Listen. Listen. Do not go into the interview with any objective or intent other than to listen" [V]. "Gather quotes to add authenticity to the story" [V] (Handout B, "Listen").
- **Caution.** "If someone is talking about an unhappy or painful experience show them you understand how they feel. If they don't want to talk about something, do not push the issue" [V]. "If someone is remembering a painful memory or sharing a difficult story be mindful of their mental status. Make sure you conclude the interview with a discussion about casual things or more recent events to bring them back out of the moment. Make sure the appropriate mental health professionals are available if needed" [V] (Handout B, "Caution").

The handout's second page structures the interview itself (Handout B, second page):

- **Beginning.** "Introduce yourself and any other team members. If this involves an injury of any sort, ask them how they are doing. Ask them if they have ever heard of an FLA and give a brief overview of the process" [V]. "If using a note taker, explain their role in the interview and assure them they can read any of the notes" [V]. Casual openers: "How was your fire season?" "How has your summer/fall/winter/spring been?" "How are things going lately?" [V].
- **During.** "Remember to give them space to talk and give room for silence. Think about what you have heard and give them time to reflect" [V]. Follow-up questions come to mind while listening and "will help you get more information" [V]. Questions "to help gather information if you need ideas" [V]: "What are you able to tell me about your experience?" "If you were sitting around with family (kids, buddies, etc.) what would you have told them?" "What was your gut telling you?" "What surprised you the most?" "What do you feel you learned from this event? What do you think the agency needs to learn?" [V].
- **Concluding.** "When the person you are interviewing has told their story and doesn't have much more to add you can begin to conclude the interview" [V]. "It is often helpful for you to tell them what you heard in their interview. To paraphrase it back to them to make sure you got it right. Give them a chance to correct any misinterpretations" [V]. "Share any notes or quotes you might have captured if they are interested" [V]. "Remind them you will go back and write out their story and they will get to review what was written before it goes up the chain of command" [V]. "Exchange contact information so if they think of anything else they can share it with you or if you have any follow up questions you can reach them" [V]. "Remember to make sure they are mentally in a good place before you leave" [V] (Handout B, "Concluding the Interview").

## Part XVII: Storytelling tips (Handout E)

Handout E gives working tips in three groups (Handout E, "Tips for Facilitated Learning Analysis Storytelling"):

- **Collecting good information during interviews and site visits.** "Look and listen – write down sounds, colors and smells when in interviews or site visits" [V] and get personal background on the main players; "Take photos generously" [V], including visual reminders that might not seem important at the time; ask clarifying questions, and "Generally it's best to have one person to do most of the asking and then let the other interviewers ask follow-up questions toward the end" [V]; reflect with the team straight after each interview, highlighting key information, themes and quotes [AP]. The three "storytelling critical elements (empathy pathways)" to weave in are the differences between what the main player believes is true and what is actually true, between what they want to do and what they are expected to do, and between their inner and external goals [AP] [BT] (citing Lisa Cron, *Wired for Story*, p. 130).
- **Working with an FLA team.** "Have one person write the story; don't divide it up between team members" [V]; give the writer time without micromanaging; "be wary about editing at the sentence level as a group" [V], saving polish for the final draft [AP].
- **Writing the story.** "Start strong" [V]; describe the smells, tastes and sounds, and what the main players were feeling and why [AP]; capture quotes from expressive speakers, but "Be careful however, to not limit your perspective to just that of these expressive speakers" [V]; "Don't be concerned about capturing all the details. A story in an FLA is not an exhaustive learning product" [V]; read the story aloud to the team and check the critical elements [AP].

The handout's examples are a site diagram from the Tarkio Fire, I-90 Complex Shelter Deployment Investigation ("one of the original efforts to take a more doctrinal approach to accident reviews" [V]), an excerpt from the 2018 Horse Park Fire Entrapment FLA ("The wind is gusting and they feel a wave of heat on their backs as they pass campsite 5" [V]), and a participant's quote from the 2011 Pagami Creek Fire Entrapments FLA held only as an image [AE] (Handout E, captions).

## Key concepts and definitions (from Glossary)

| Term | Source definition |
|---|---|
| Accountability | "An account is something you tell and learn from. Accountability is taking that story and looking towards the future..." [V] (Glossary, "Accountability"). |
| Accountabilism | Claiming to learn from accounts but then punishing via judgmental language or training-as-punishment [AP] (Glossary, "Accountabilism"). |
| Conditions | "Factors which affected pertinent decisions and actions that took place during the event like environmental conditions... as well as social, cultural, and political influences" [V] (Glossary, "Conditions"). |
| Culpability | "Responsibility for wrongdoing or failure; moral/legal/criminal culpability" — what people often mean when they say *accountability* [V] [BT] (Glossary, "Culpability", credited in the source to Webster). |
| Dialogue | "A conversation with a center, not sides. The intention of dialogue is to reach a new understanding. In dialogue, one seeks to uncover a base of shared meaning..." [V] [BT] (Glossary, "Dialogue", quoting Isaacs 1999). |
| ETTO (Efficiency-Thoroughness Trade-Off) | "If demands to productivity or performance are high, thoroughness is reduced until the productivity goals are met. If demands to safety are high, efficiency is reduced until the safety goals are met" [V] [BT] (Glossary, "Efficiency-Thoroughness Trade-Off", quoting Hollnagel). |
| GAP | "The difference between what administrators think is going on and what is really going on in the field" [V] (Glossary, "GAP"). |
| High Reliability Organization | "An infrastructure for organizations utilizing five principles with the intent of minimizing catastrophic events: preoccupation with failure, reluctance to oversimplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience and deference to expertise" [V] [BT] (Glossary, "High Reliability Organization", citing Weick & Sutcliffe 2007). |
| Networked causality | "The combined total of those conditions that collectively influenced the event or outcome" [V] (Glossary, "Networked causality"). |
| Recognition primed decision making | "A model people can use experience to generate a plausible option as the first one they consider" [V] [BT] (Glossary, "Recognition primed decision making", citing Gary Klein). |
| Restorative justice | "An element of just culture which aims to restore the status of the individual involved and heal relationships and injuries of victims and the wider community in the wake of an ethical breach" [V] [BT] (Glossary, "Restorative justice", citing Dekker). |
| Retributive justice | "A post event/accident approach which focuses on determining the proper treatment of those who have breached certain standards of conduct. It is focused on the errors or violations of individuals" [V] [BT] (Glossary, "Retributive justice", citing Dekker). |
| Safety-vs-production | "The dynamic tension between an organization's desire to accomplish work (production) and its desire to keep its people free from harm or injury" [V] (Glossary, "Safety-vs-production"). |
| Sensemaking | "The process of creating situational awareness and understanding situations of high complexity or uncertainty to make decisions" [V] (Glossary, "Sensemaking"). |
| Sharp end / blunt end | Sharp end = workers directly confronting risk; blunt end = supervisors and administrators with strategic risk management and time-rich decision environments [AP] (Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors"). |
| Storytelling | "The process in which we seek to take an event and share the knowledge and wisdom the participants of the unintended outcome experienced. An FLA's story is a factual description of what occurred told in a manner that seeks to share sensory detail..." [V] (Glossary, "Storytelling"). |

A pull quote in the Glossary pages, from Tom Harbor, former USFS Fire Director, quoting Visa founder Dee Hock: "'Simple clear purpose and principles give rise to complex intelligent behavior. Complex rules and regulations give rise to simple stupid behavior.' We are focused on defining those simple clear principles that will encourage complex intelligent behavior" [V] [BT] (Glossary, pull quote, citing *Wildland Fire Suppression: Foundational Doctrine*, June 2005).

- **David Marx** — approving; *Patient Safety and the "Just Culture"* (2001) is in Recommended Reading [BT] (Recommended Reading).
- **Paul Chamberlain** — named as the originator of the FLA: "Paul Chamberlin stated the intent of a FLA was to 'improve performance by capitalizing on the shared experiences of participants.'" [V] [BT] (Part 9, "FLA Learning Products"). (Note: the source spells the name "Chamberlin" in this passage and "Chamberlain" in the Preface; the Preface spelling is used here.)
- **Pull-quote voices** — approving; quoted beside the text without further citation: Kevin A. Plank on trust; Preston Cline, academic reviewer for the Eicks Learning Review, on risks traded for unseen risks; former Chief Tom Tidwell on learning as a core value and on review information not being used for discipline; Ivan Pupulidy on networks of influence; David Woods on the past seeming incredible after an accident; Dr. Jennifer Ziegler on creating a movement; NAFRI's Learning from Unintended Outcomes Workshop on the Lessons Learned Analysis; Tom Harbor quoting Dee Hock on simple principles [BT] (Parts 1, 3, 7, 9; Glossary).

## Positions the source explicitly frames against

- **The blame-and-rule-tightening response to accidents.** "Following this logic, all that's needed are better rules or better compliance. And that's the end of story — until the next accident. History has shown us that this approach is not only ineffective for improving safety related to a specific accident, but also damaging to the overall learning culture" [V] (Part 1, "Systems Thinking").
- **The criminal-justice meaning of accountability.** "In the criminal justice arena accountability means punishments and correction. In our Just Culture, accountability means creating the space for each person involved to provide an honest account..." [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture").
- **Root-cause analysis in complex systems.** The Glossary defines RCA at the simple/complicated end of the spectrum and points to Appendix B for the deep-dive critique [AP] (Glossary, "Root Cause or Root Cause Analysis"; Appendix B). The SAI process is explicitly named as the root-cause-based alternative the FLA/LR family departs from (Part 2, "The tools").
- **Causal statements in accident reports.** "FLAs must avoid causal statements" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned"). "Cause isn't something investigators 'find' or 'discover'; cause is always something we create..." [V] (Appendix B, "A Deeper Dive into Causal Factors").
- **Recommendations as the default output.** "In many circumstances, recommendations actually interfere with learning. Often recommendations, when implemented, add complexity to the workplace, which has the paradoxical effect of increasing risk" [V] (Part 5, "Recommendations vs Lessons Learned").
- **Counterfactual reasoning.** "FLA teams must guard against making counterfactual arguments" [V] (Part 9, "Avoid Counterfactual Arguments").
- **Severity-of-outcome as the criterion for review-team size.** "Often, the more 'serious the accident,' the more resources are put toward the review team. This tendency may pretermit stellar learning opportunities" [V] (Part 3, "Starting the process").
- **The machine metaphor for understanding social systems.** "The machine metaphor is not as widely applicable as our culture seems to give it credit for" [V] (Part 10, "What is a Learning Review?").
- **The Fundamental Attribution Error in incident analysis.** "Blaming employees can be a form of the Fundamental Attribution Error" [V] (Part 3, "Administrative assurance of no punitive actions").
- **The "we just need more training" reflex.** "When 'we just need more training' comes up… Try to dig deeper. Sometimes, that is the answer, but sometimes it's not. If you don't have on your PPE because you can't do your job properly and wear it, it's a bigger issue than training" [V] (Part 6, "Suggestions to FLA Facilitator for the Group Dialogue Session").
- **"You've got nothing to fear if you've done nothing wrong."** "The attitude expressed in the quote above is a threat and has no place in an FLA" [V] (Part 1, "Just Culture", box).
- **Signed witness statements and recorded interviews.** "FLA Teams never collect written witness statements or record interviews" [V] (Part 6, "No Signed Witness Statements: An FLA Commitment").
- **Asking "why" in interviews.** "Never ask WHY; instead ask HOW or WHAT" [V] (Handout B, "Be Curious").
- **Agreement as a sign of a good dialogue.** "FEAR THE FUSION. NOT THE CONFUSION" [V] (Part 6, box).
- **Reviews that stop at the scene.** FLAs "tend to focus almost solely on actions and actors at the scene" [V], and the Delegating Official is asked whether they are "the elephant in the room" (Part 5, "Are you the elephant in the room?").

## Citation and source-integrity notes

The PDF is born-digital from MS Word. The body of this reference was first read from a pymupdf4llm 0.2.9 conversion, which dropped the text of framed sidebars, pull quotes and boxed worksheets (about 11% of the PDF's longer lines). The source was re-converted on 2026-10-16 (PyMuPDF text blocks; see the source card), and every passage the re-conversion restored was then read in full and added to this reference (see the Coverage line). The re-conversion reads a side box after the body text beside it, so a quotation that runs past a box at the foot of a page shows as `missing` or `page` in check-verbatim (Part 1 "Just Culture", Part 5 "Forming the FLA team", Part 9 "Serious Crimes"); each was checked by hand. Page anchors were not preserved by the conversion, so citations use `(Part N, "Section name")`, `(Appendix X, "Section name")`, `(Handout X, "Section name")`, and `(Glossary, "Term")` styles per the source's own structural divisions.

Text held only as images or drawn graphics, found with a tesseract OCR of all 98 pages checked line by line against the converted text: (1) three of Handout C's five boxes (confirmation bias, outcome bias, hindsight bias) are drawn as graphics and are described in Part X from the OCR and a render, as [AP]; (2) Appendix F, the Restorative Just Culture Checklist, is two raster pages and is described in Part XIV from the OCR, as [AP]; (3) a three-principles graphic on PDF p. 8 restates Part 1's principles, and a graphic on PDF p. 58 ("Dynamics of Influence & Change") states that the goal is to understand the internal and external pressures that influenced decisions and actions; both were read and neither adds a claim not made in the text; (4) photo captions inside images, covers and screenshots of example reports (PDF pp. 12, 19, 34, 43, 47, 53) and a quote image from the 2011 Pagami Creek Fire Entrapments FLA (PDF p. 91) are illustrative and not carried. The Part 4 process graphic, the Five Hows graphic and the Learning Review outline are text, but the converted text gives their labels in drawing order; their order here was read from renders of PDF pp. 22, 46 and 59. Restored minor items that were read and not carried individually: the 25-minute introductory video and the Gregg Creek video links, the Lessons Learned Center YouTube and story-map links, and the Elkhorn 2 caption's final sentence, which is cut off by its frame in the PDF.

Image classification was deferred — this was a text-only ingest; the `ingesting-images` skill can be applied later to classify diagrams and the Five Hows / Watch Outs graphics if they are needed downstream.

The PDF (3.5 MB) was promoted from `sources/ingest/` to `sources/original/` and is shipped in the open profile because the document is in the public domain under 17 USC §105 (US federal-employee work, hosted on a US Government S3 bucket, no copyright notice).
